statement: If a positive [measurable](c:measurable-function) function $L$ is [slowly varying](c:slowly-varying-function), then $L(\lambda x)/L(x) \to 1$ [uniformly](c:uniform-convergence) for $\lambda$ in every compact interval $[c,d] \subset (0,\infty)$. The same holds for a [regularly varying](c:regularly-varying-function) $f(x) = x^\rho L(x)$ with limit $\lambda^\rho$.

hypotheses.text: $L\colon [a,\infty) \to (0,\infty)$ is Lebesgue [measurable](c:measurable-function).
$L(\lambda x)/L(x) \to 1$ as $x \to \infty$ for every $\lambda > 0$, so $L$ is [slowly varying](c:slowly-varying-function).
$[c,d]$ is a compact [interval](c:interval) with $0 < c \le d < \infty$.

conclusion: $\sup_{c \le \lambda \le d} |L(\lambda x)/L(x) - 1| \to 0$ as $x \to \infty$. For $f(x) = x^\rho L(x)$, also $\sup_{c \le \lambda \le d} |f(\lambda x)/f(x) - \lambda^\rho| \to 0$.

proofs.name: Limit superior of bad sets
proofs.slogan: Assume that uniformity fails, build bad sets of shifts with measure bounded below, and find one shift where pointwise convergence fails.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, for slowly varying $L$ and for regularly varying $f = x^\rho L$ with any $\rho \in \mathbb{R}$.

roles.why: Measurability makes the bad sets Lebesgue measurable, so their measures and the reverse Fatou bound make sense.
Pointwise slow variation at one fixed shift is the statement that the final point contradicts.
A compact interval of ratios becomes a bounded interval $[-K,K]$ of additive shifts.

steps.slogan: Pass to the additive form $h(u) = \log L(e^u)$ on a bounded interval of shifts.
steps.detail: Put $K = \max(|\log c|, |\log d|)$. Since $|e^y - 1| \le e^{|y|} - 1$, it suffices to show $\sup_{|v| \le K} |h(u+v) - h(u)| \to 0$. Slow variation says $h(u+v) - h(u) \to 0$ for each fixed $v$.

steps.slogan: Assume failure and cover the shift interval by two families of bad sets.
steps.detail: Take $\varepsilon > 0$, $u_n \to \infty$ and $|v_n| \le K$ with $|h(u_n+v_n) - h(u_n)| \ge \varepsilon$. The shifts $y \in [-K,K]$ that move $h$ by at least $\varepsilon/2$ away from $h(u_n)$ form $A_n$, and those that move it away from $h(u_n+v_n)$ form $B_n$. The triangle inequality gives $A_n \cup B_n = [-K,K]$, so one of them has [Lebesgue measure](c:lebesgue-measure) at least $K$.

steps.slogan: Translate the second family so that both families start from points that tend to infinity.
steps.detail: Set $w_n = u_n + v_n \to \infty$ and $C_n = B_n - v_n \subset [-2K, 2K]$. Translation invariance gives $m(C_n) = m(B_n)$, and $C_n$ is the set of shifts $z$ with $|h(w_n+z) - h(w_n)| \ge \varepsilon/2$.

steps.slogan: Bound the measure of the [limit superior](c:limit-superior) of the bad sets from below.
steps.detail: Along an infinite set of indices with $m(A_n) \ge K$, or with $m(C_n) \ge K$, the indicators are bounded by the indicator of $[-2K,2K]$. The reverse Fatou inequality gives $m(\limsup A_n) \ge \limsup m(A_n) \ge K > 0$, and the same for $C_n$.

steps.slogan: Pick a point in the limit superior and contradict pointwise slow variation.
steps.detail: A point $y^*$ of $\limsup A_n$ gives $|h(u_n + y^*) - h(u_n)| \ge \varepsilon/2$ for infinitely many $n$, with $u_n \to \infty$. This contradicts slow variation at the fixed shift $y^*$. The sets $C_n$ give the same contradiction along $w_n$. The bound $\lambda^\rho \le \max(c^\rho, d^\rho)$ then gives the regularly varying case.

Such an $L$ changes more slowly than every power: $x^{-\varepsilon}L(x)\to0$ and $x^{\varepsilon}L(x)\to\infty$ for every $\varepsilon>0$.

statement: A positive [measurable](c:measurable-function) function $L$ on $[a,\infty)$ is [slowly varying](c:slowly-varying-function) if and only if $L(x) = c(x)\exp\left(\int_a^x \varepsilon(u)\,du/u\right)$ with $c(x) \to c_0 \in (0,\infty)$ and $\varepsilon(x) \to 0$.

hypotheses.text: $L\colon [a,\infty) \to (0,\infty)$ is [measurable](c:measurable-function).
For the direct part, $L$ is [slowly varying](c:slowly-varying-function): $L(\lambda x)/L(x) \to 1$ for every $\lambda > 0$.

For the converse, $L(x) = c(x)\exp\left(\int_a^x \varepsilon(u)\,du/u\right)$ with measurable $c$ of [limit](c:limit-of-a-function) $c_0 \in (0,\infty)$ and measurable $\varepsilon$ of limit $0$, bounded on bounded intervals.

conclusion: Each condition implies the other. Multiplication by $x^\rho$ gives the same statement for a [regularly varying](c:regularly-varying-function) $f$ of index $\rho$, with $\varepsilon$ replaced by a function $\delta \to \rho$.

proofs.name: Integral of the Karamata ratio
proofs.slogan: Karamata's theorem gives x L(x)/F(x) → 1, and integrating the logarithmic derivative of F turns this ratio into the representation.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem: both directions for slowly varying $L$ and for regularly varying $f$ of any index $\rho$.

roles.why: Measurability lets Karamata's integral theorem apply and makes c and ε measurable.
Slow variation gives the Karamata ratio limit $b(x) \to 1$.
The representation gives the converse through a bound on the integral of ε over [x, λx].

steps.slogan: Apply Karamata's integral theorem with index $0$ to get the ratio $b(x) \to 1$.
steps.detail: $L$ is bounded on bounded parts of some $[X,\infty)$, and $F(x) = \int_X^x L$ satisfies $b(x) = xL(x)/F(x) \to 1$. Beyond a point $x_1 > X$, $F \ge F(x_1) > 0$, so $b$ is measurable and bounded on bounded intervals.

steps.slogan: Integrate the derivative of the [absolutely continuous](c:absolutely-continuous-function) function $\log F$.
steps.detail: The Lebesgue differentiation theorem gives $F' = L$ almost everywhere, so $(\log F)' = b(s)/s$ almost everywhere. The fundamental theorem of calculus gives $\log F(x) = \log F(x_1) + \int_{x_1}^x b(s)\,ds/s$ for $x \ge x_1$.

steps.slogan: Rewrite $L = bF/x$ as the representation with $c = bF(x_1)/x_1$ and $\varepsilon = b - 1$.
steps.detail: Since $1/x = x_1^{-1}\exp(-\int_{x_1}^x ds/s)$, $L(x) = b(x)\,(F(x_1)/x_1)\exp(\int_{x_1}^x (b(s)-1)\,ds/s)$. Setting $c = L$ and $\varepsilon = 0$ on $[a, x_1)$ extends the formula to all $x \ge a$, with $c \to F(x_1)/x_1$ and $\varepsilon \to 0$.

steps.slogan: Bound the integral of $\varepsilon$ over $[x, \lambda x]$ to show that a representation forces slow variation.
steps.detail: $L(\lambda x)/L(x) = (c(\lambda x)/c(x))\exp(\int_x^{\lambda x} \varepsilon(u)\,du/u)$. The first factor tends to $1$, and the integral is at most $\sup_{u \ge \min(x,\lambda x)} |\varepsilon(u)|\cdot|\log \lambda|$ in absolute value, which tends to $0$.

steps.slogan: Transfer both directions to [regularly varying](c:regularly-varying-function) functions through the factor $x^\rho$.
steps.detail: If $f$ has index $\rho$, then $x^{-\rho} f$ is slowly varying, and $x^\rho = a^\rho\exp(\int_a^x \rho\,du/u)$ gives $f(x) = a^\rho c(x)\exp(\int_a^x (\rho + \varepsilon(u))\,du/u)$. The converse bound applied to $\delta - \rho$ gives the reverse direction.

concepts.c:slowly-varying-function: Slow variation is the property that the representation characterizes.
concepts.c:limit-of-a-function: The limits of c and ε at infinity are the defining conditions of the representation.
concepts.c:absolutely-continuous-function: Absolute continuity of log F lets the proof integrate its derivative b(s)/s.
concepts.c:regularly-varying-function: Regularly varying functions get the same representation with a drift δ → ρ.

For every $\lambda$ in a measurable set $\Lambda \subset (0,\infty)$ of positive [Lebesgue measure](c:lebesgue-measure), the [limit](c:limit-of-a-function) $g(\lambda) = \lim_{t\to\infty} f(\lambda t)/f(t)$ exists in $(0,\infty)$.

proofs.name: Steinhaus group argument
proofs.slogan: The shifts with a limit form a subgroup containing a set of positive measure, so Steinhaus' theorem makes it all of the real line.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, for every measurable set of scale factors with positive measure.

roles.why: Measurability makes the limit function φ measurable, which forces it to be linear.
The ratio limits put a set of positive measure inside the group of good shifts.

steps.slogan: Pass to $h(u) = \log f(e^u)$ and show that the good shifts form a [subgroup](c:subgroup).
steps.detail: Let $K$ be the set of $v$ for which $\varphi(v) = \lim_{u\to\infty}(h(u+v) - h(u))$ exists. Splitting $h(u+v+w) - h(u)$ at the point $u + w$ shows that $K$ is closed under sums and negatives, and that $\varphi$ is additive on $K$.

steps.slogan: Use Steinhaus' theorem to show that the group of good shifts is all of $\mathbb{R}$.
steps.detail: $K$ contains $\log\Lambda$, which has positive measure by the change of variables formula. Steinhaus' theorem puts an interval $(-\delta,\delta)$ inside the [difference set](c:difference-set) $\log\Lambda - \log\Lambda \subset K$, and every real number is a finite sum of elements of this interval.

steps.slogan: Show that the limit function $\varphi$ is measurable as a limit along integers.
steps.detail: For every real $v$, $\varphi(v) = \lim_n (h(n+v) - h(n))$ along the integers $n$, and each map $v \mapsto h(n+v) - h(n)$ is measurable. So $\varphi$ is a measurable [group homomorphism](c:group-homomorphism) of $(\mathbb{R}, +)$.

steps.slogan: Prove that the measurable additive function $\varphi$ is linear.
steps.detail: Some set $\{|\varphi| \le N\} \cap [0,1]$ has positive measure, so Steinhaus' theorem bounds $|\varphi|$ by $2N$ on an interval $(-\eta,\eta)$. With $\varphi(r) = r\varphi(1)$ for rational $r$, the bound $|\varphi(x - r)| = |\varphi(q(x-r))|/q \le 2N/q$ gives $\varphi(x) = x\varphi(1)$.

steps.slogan: Convert the linear limit back to the multiplicative ratio $\lambda^\rho$.
steps.detail: With $\rho = \varphi(1)$, $f(\lambda t)/f(t) = \exp(h(\log t + \log\lambda) - h(\log t)) \to \exp(\rho\log\lambda) = \lambda^\rho$ for every $\lambda > 0$. So $f$ is regularly varying with index $\rho$.

new_concepts.reminder: A regularly varying function grows like a power $x^\rho$ times a slowly varying factor at infinity.
new_concepts.definition: A positive [measurable function](c:measurable-function) $f$ on $(0,\infty)$ is regularly varying at infinity with index $\rho\in\mathbb{R}$ when $\lim_{x\to\infty}f(\lambda x)/f(x)=\lambda^\rho$ for every $\lambda>0$. Every such $f$ has the form $f(x)=x^\rho L(x)$, where $L$ is a [slowly varying function](c:slowly-varying-function).

statement: If $f$ is [regularly varying](c:regularly-varying-function) with index $\alpha$, then its [integral](c:lebesgue-integral) is [asymptotically equivalent](c:asymptotic) to $x f(x)/(\alpha+1)$ when $\alpha > -1$, and its tail integral to $x f(x)/(-\alpha-1)$ when $\alpha < -1$. Conversely, these ratio limits force regular variation.

hypotheses.text: $f\colon [a,\infty) \to (0,\infty)$ is [measurable](c:measurable-function) and [regularly varying](c:regularly-varying-function) with index $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$.
For the converse, $g > 0$ is [integrable](c:integrable-function) on bounded intervals and $x g(x)/\int_a^x g \to c \in (0,\infty)$, or the same holds for the tail integral.

conclusion: $f$ is bounded on bounded parts of some $[X,\infty)$. With $F(x) = \int_X^x f$, $x f(x)/F(x) \to \alpha + 1$ if $\alpha > -1$ and $\to 0$ if $\alpha = -1$, and $x f(x)/\int_x^\infty f \to -\alpha - 1$ if $\alpha < -1$. Conversely, $g$ is regularly varying with index $c - 1$, or $-c - 1$ in the tail form.

proofs.name: Dyadic blocks and the uniform convergence theorem
proofs.slogan: Compare integrals over dyadic blocks with the value of f at the block start, then divide two block limits.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem: the cases $\alpha > -1$, $\alpha = -1$ and $\alpha < -1$, and both forms of the converse.

roles.why: Regular variation controls f on dyadic blocks and gives the limit of block integrals.
The ratio limit is the derivative of $\log F$ times $x$, so it integrates to regular variation of $F$.

steps.slogan: Bound f on dyadic blocks with the uniform convergence theorem.
steps.detail: Uniform convergence on $[1,2]$ gives $X$ and $M$ with $f(\lambda t) \le M f(t)$ for $t \ge X$ and $\lambda \in [1,2]$. A chain of such bounds gives $f(s) \le M^{n+1} f(X)$ on $[2^n X, 2^{n+1} X]$, so $f$ is integrable on bounded intervals.

steps.slogan: Write block integrals as averages of $f(xu)/f(x)$ and pass to the limit.
steps.detail: The substitution $s = xu$ gives $F(\lambda x) - F(x) = x f(x) \int_1^\lambda f(xu)/f(x)\,du$. [Uniform convergence](c:uniform-convergence) on the compact $u$-interval gives the limit $\int_1^\lambda u^\alpha\,du$ for the ratio $(F(\lambda x) - F(x))/(x f(x))$.

steps.slogan: For $\alpha > -1$, show that $F$ diverges and varies regularly with index $\alpha + 1$, then divide.
steps.detail: Since $f(2s) \ge f(s)/2$ eventually, the dyadic block integrals do not decrease and $F \to \infty$. Pointwise bounds $(1 \pm \varepsilon)\lambda^\alpha f(s)$ for $f(\lambda s)$ give $F(\lambda x)/F(x) \to \lambda^{\alpha+1}$. Dividing the two limits for $F(2x) - F(x)$ gives $x f(x)/F(x) \to \alpha + 1$.

steps.slogan: For $\alpha < -1$, sum a geometric series of blocks and divide the tail limits.
steps.detail: Since $f(2s) \le \eta f(s)$ with $2\eta < 1$, the block integrals decay geometrically and the tail integral $G$ is finite. The same pointwise bounds give $G(\lambda x)/G(x) \to \lambda^{\alpha+1}$, and dividing the limits for $G(x) - G(2x)$ gives $x f(x)/G(x) \to -\alpha - 1$.

steps.slogan: For $\alpha = -1$, bound the Karamata ratio by $1/\log K$ for every $K$.
steps.detail: The block limit with $\lambda = 1/K$ gives $F(x) \ge F(x) - F(x/K) \sim x f(x) \log K$. So $\limsup x f(x)/F(x) \le 1/\log K$ for every $K > 1$, and the ratio tends to $0$. The tail integral is treated in the same way with $\lambda = K$.

steps.slogan: Integrate $(\log F)' = b(s)/s$ to recover regular variation from the ratio limit.
steps.detail: $F$ is [absolutely continuous](c:absolutely-continuous-function) with $F' = g$ almost everywhere, so $\log F(\lambda x) - \log F(x) = \int_x^{\lambda x} b(s)\,ds/s \to c \log \lambda$. Then $F$ varies regularly with index $c$, and $g = bF/x$ with index $c - 1$. The tail form gives index $-c - 1$.

steps.slogan: Collect the three cases of the direct part and the converse into the theorem.
steps.detail: Local boundedness comes from the dyadic bound. The cases $\alpha > -1$, $\alpha = -1$ and $\alpha < -1$ give the three ratio limits, so in each case the integral is [asymptotically equivalent](c:asymptotic) to its prediction. The converse step gives the reverse implication.

concepts.c:uniform-convergence: Uniform convergence of f(xu)/f(x) lets the limit pass inside block integrals.

proofs.name: Bounds from the Karamata representation
proofs.slogan: Write f through its Karamata representation and bound the constant factor by A and the drift by ρ ± δ.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, for every index $\rho$, every $A > 1$ and every $\delta > 0$.

roles.why: Regular variation gives the Karamata representation with a drift that tends to ρ.
The constants $A$ and $\delta$ fix how close $c$ and the drift must be to their limits.

steps.slogan: Write $f$ as $c(x)\exp(\int_a^x \eta(u)\,du/u)$ with the Karamata representation theorem.
steps.detail: The [limit](c:limit-of-a-function) of $c$ is $c_0 \in (0,\infty)$ and the drift $\eta(u)$ tends to $\rho$. Then $f(y)/f(x) = (c(y)/c(x))\exp(\int_x^y \eta(u)\,du/u)$ for all $x, y \ge a$.

steps.slogan: Choose $X$ so that $c$ stays within a factor $\sqrt{A}$ of $c_0$ and the drift within $\delta$ of $\rho$.
steps.detail: Beyond such an $X$ the ratio $c(y)/c(x)$ lies in $[A^{-1}, A]$, and $|\eta(u) - \rho| \le \delta$ for every $u \ge X$.

steps.slogan: Bound the [exponential](c:exponential-function) factor by powers of $y/x$ in the cases $y \ge x$ and $y < x$.
steps.detail: Integrating $(\rho \pm \delta)/u$ between $x$ and $y$ gives $(\rho \pm \delta)\log(y/x)$. So the exponential factor lies between the smaller and the larger of $(y/x)^{\rho+\delta}$ and $(y/x)^{\rho-\delta}$, whatever the order of $x$ and $y$.

steps.slogan: Multiply the two bounds and read off the one-sided Potter form.
steps.detail: The product gives both inequalities for $x, y \ge X$. With $A = 1 + \varepsilon/2$, $\delta = \varepsilon$, $x = t$ and $y = \lambda t$ for $\lambda \ge 1$, it gives $(1-\varepsilon)\lambda^{\rho-\varepsilon} < f(\lambda t)/f(t) < (1+\varepsilon)\lambda^{\rho+\varepsilon}$. The [slowly varying](c:slowly-varying-function) part of $f$ is what costs the margin $\delta$.

statement: For a non-decreasing $U$, the growth $U(x) \sim c\,x^\alpha L(x)/\Gamma(1+\alpha)$ at infinity is equivalent to the behaviour $\hat U(s) \sim c\,s^{-\alpha} L(1/s)$ of its [Laplace-Stieltjes transform](c:laplace-transform) at $0$, for a [slowly varying](c:slowly-varying-function) $L$.

hypotheses.text: $U$ is [non-decreasing](c:monotone-function) and right-continuous on $\mathbb{R}$, with $U(x) = 0$ for $x < 0$.
$L$ is [slowly varying](c:slowly-varying-function).
$c \ge 0$ and $\alpha \ge 0$.

conclusion: $U(x) \sim c\,x^\alpha L(x)/\Gamma(1+\alpha)$ as $x \to \infty$ if and only if $\hat U(s) \sim c\,s^{-\alpha}L(1/s)$ as $s \downarrow 0$, with $o$-relations when $c = 0$.

proofs.name: Dominated convergence and Karamata's polynomial method
proofs.slogan: Prove the Abelian direction by dominated convergence and the Tauberian direction by testing scaled measures against polynomials in e^(−y).
proofs.scope: The full equivalence for all $c \ge 0$ and $\alpha \ge 0$.

roles.why: Monotonicity makes $dU$ a positive measure, so the polynomial sandwich and the bound $U(x) \le e\,\hat U(1/x)$ hold.
Slow variation gives the pointwise limits, and Potter's bounds for $L$ give the domination.
With $\alpha \ge 0$ the dominating function $t^{\alpha - 1/2}$ is integrable at $0$, and the limit law $\nu_\alpha$ exists.

steps.slogan: Write $\hat U(s) = \int_0^\infty e^{-t} U(t/s)\,dt$.
steps.detail: This is Tonelli's theorem applied to $e^{-sy} = s\int_y^\infty e^{-sx}\,dx$, a [Stieltjes integral](c:stieltjes-integral) turned into a Lebesgue integral.

steps.slogan: From growth of U to behaviour of the transform: dominated convergence.
steps.detail: The integrand $s^\alpha U(t/s)/L(1/s)$ tends to $c\,t^\alpha/\Gamma(1+\alpha)$. Potter's bounds dominate it by $2C(t^{\alpha+1/2} + t^{\alpha-1/2})$ for $t \ge sX$, and the part $t < sX$ tends to $0$. The integral of $e^{-t} t^\alpha$ is $\Gamma(1+\alpha)$, the [Gamma function](c:gamma-function).

steps.slogan: For $c = 0$ the Tauberian direction is the bound $U(x) \le e\,\hat U(1/x)$.
steps.detail: On $[0, x]$ the weight $e^{-y/x}$ is at least $e^{-1}$, so $U(x) = \mu([0,x]) \le e\,\hat U(1/x) = o(x^\alpha L(x))$.

steps.slogan: Rescale the measure dU so that its transforms converge to the transform of a fixed limit measure.
steps.detail: $\nu_x(B) = \mu(xB)/\hat U(1/x)$ has transform $\hat U(t/x)/\hat U(1/x) \to t^{-\alpha}$, which is the transform of $\nu_\alpha(dy) = y^{\alpha-1}dy/\Gamma(\alpha)$.

steps.slogan: Squeeze the indicator of $[0, 1]$ between two [polynomials](c:polynomial) in $e^{-y}$ (times $e^{-y}$).
steps.detail: The transforms converge for every polynomial in $e^{-y}$. Continuous functions $g_1 \le h \le g_2$ that differ only near $z = 1/e$, followed by Weierstrass approximation, give polynomials whose integrals against $\nu_\alpha$ differ by at most $5\eta$.

steps.slogan: Read off $U(x)/\hat U(1/x) \to \nu_\alpha([0,1]) = 1/\Gamma(1+\alpha)$.
steps.detail: Combine the limit with (b) at $s = 1/x$. This gives the [asymptotic equivalence](c:asymptotic) (a).

statement: If $X \ge 0$ has a [regularly varying](c:regularly-varying-function) tail of index $-\alpha$ and an [independent](c:independent-random-variables) $Y \ge 0$ has a finite [moment](c:moment) of order $\alpha + \varepsilon$, then $P(XY > x)$ is [asymptotically equivalent](c:asymptotic) to $\mathbb{E}(Y^\alpha)\,P(X > x)$.

hypotheses.text: $X \ge 0$ and $P(X > x)$ is [regularly varying](c:regularly-varying-function) with index $-\alpha$ for some $\alpha > 0$.
$Y \ge 0$ is [independent](c:independent-random-variables) of $X$.
$\mathbb{E}(Y^{\alpha+\varepsilon}) < \infty$ for some $\varepsilon > 0$, a [moment](c:moment) condition.

conclusion: $P(XY > x)/P(X > x) \to \mathbb{E}(Y^\alpha)$ as $x \to \infty$. If $P(Y > 0) > 0$, the tail of $XY$ is regularly varying with index $-\alpha$.

proofs.name: Conditioning and Potter domination
proofs.slogan: Condition on the light factor, dominate the tail ratio with Potter's bounds, and kill the large factor values with Markov's inequality.
proofs.scope: The whole lemma, for every $\alpha > 0$ and $\varepsilon > 0$.

roles.why: Regular variation gives the pointwise limit of the tail ratio and Potter's bounds.
Independence lets the product tail be an integral over the law of Y.
The moment of order $\alpha + \varepsilon$ makes the Potter bound integrable and controls large values of $Y$.

steps.slogan: Condition on $Y$ to write the tail ratio as an integral against the [law](c:probability-distribution) of $Y$.
steps.detail: By independence and Fubini's theorem, $P(XY > x)/P(X > x) = \int_{(0,\infty)} \bar F(x/y)/\bar F(x)\,G(dy)$. For each fixed $y > 0$ the integrand tends to $y^\alpha$.

steps.slogan: Dominate the integrand for $y \le x/x_0$ with Potter's bounds and pass to the limit.
steps.detail: With $0 < \delta < \min(\varepsilon, \alpha)$, Potter's bounds give $\bar F(x/y)/\bar F(x) \le 2(1 + y^{\alpha+\varepsilon})$ for $y \le x/x_0$. This bound is integrable, so dominated convergence gives the limit $\mathbb{E}(Y^\alpha)$ for this part.

steps.slogan: Bound the part $y > x/x_0$ by Markov's inequality and the slow decay of the tail.
steps.detail: This part is at most $P(Y > x/x_0)/\bar F(x) \le \mathbb{E}(Y^{\alpha+\varepsilon})(x_0/x)^{\alpha+\varepsilon}/\bar F(x)$. The lower Potter bound $\bar F(x) \ge c\,x^{-\alpha-\delta}$ makes it tend to $0$ because $\delta < \varepsilon$.

steps.slogan: Add the two parts and read off regular variation of the product tail.
steps.detail: The ratio tends to $\mathbb{E}(Y^\alpha)$, the [expected value](c:expected-value) of $Y^\alpha$. When it is positive, the ratio $P(XY > \lambda x)/P(XY > x)$ is a product of two ratios with limits $1$ and $\lambda^{-\alpha}$.

concepts.c:independent-random-variables: Independence of X and Y makes the conditioning step valid.
concepts.c:moment: A moment of Y of order above α controls the domination and the remainder.
concepts.c:asymptotic: The conclusion is an asymptotic equivalence of two tails.
concepts.c:probability-distribution: The tail ratio is integrated against the law of Y.
concepts.c:expected-value: The limit constant is the expected value of Y to the power α.

statement: If a law $F$ on $[0,\infty)$ is [subexponential](c:subexponential-distribution), then its tail decays slower than any exponential, every [convolution](c:convolution) power satisfies $\bar F^{n*} \sim n\bar F$, and $\bar F^{n*} \le K(1+\varepsilon)^n \bar F$ uniformly in $x$.

hypotheses.text: $F$ is a [distribution function](c:distribution-function) on $[0,\infty)$ with $\bar F(x) > 0$ for all $x$.
$\bar F^{2*}(x)/\bar F(x) \to 2$ as $x \to \infty$, so $F$ is [subexponential](c:subexponential-distribution).

conclusion: $\bar F(x-y)/\bar F(x) \to 1$, $e^{\varepsilon x}\bar F(x) \to \infty$, $\bar F^{n*}(x)/\bar F(x) \to n$, and for each $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $K$ with $\bar F^{n*}(x) \le K(1+\varepsilon)^n\bar F(x)$ for all $n$ and $x$.

proofs.name: Convolution recursion
proofs.slogan: Peel off one summand, compare the remaining tail with the tail of F, and control the error with long-tailedness.
proofs.scope: All four parts.

roles.why: A positive tail makes the ratios well defined, and a law on $[0,\infty)$ makes $\bar F$ monotone and the recursion valid.
The case $n = 2$ is the input for long-tailedness, for the induction and for the choice of $T$ in Kesten's bound.

steps.slogan: Peel off one summand to get $\bar F^{(n+1)*}(x) = \bar F(x) + \mathbb{E}[\bar F^{n*}(x-X); X \le x]$.
steps.detail: This follows from [independence](c:independent-random-variables) and Fubini's theorem. With $n = 1$ the hypothesis says $\mathbb{E}[\bar F(x-X); X \le x]/\bar F(x) \to 1$.

steps.slogan: Squeeze the shifted tail ratio between 1 and a bound that tends to 1.
steps.detail: Split the expectation at $X = y$ and use that $\bar F$ is [monotone](c:monotone-function). Then $1 \le \bar F(x-y)/\bar F(x) \le (\bar F^{2*}(x)/\bar F(x) - 1 - F(y))/(F(x) - F(y)) \to 1$.

steps.slogan: A tail that loses almost nothing per unit step decays slower than every exponential.
steps.detail: Long-tailedness gives $\bar F(x) \ge e^{-\varepsilon/2}\bar F(x-1)$ for large $x$. Iteration gives $e^{\varepsilon x}\bar F(x) \ge c\,e^{\varepsilon x/2} \to \infty$ for some $c > 0$.

steps.slogan: Induction on n: the recursion adds exactly one tail at each step.
steps.detail: Split the expectation at $X = x - z_0$. Away from the edge use the induction hypothesis and the case $n = 2$. Near the edge the mass $\bar F(x - z_0) - \bar F(x)$ is $o(\bar F(x))$ by long-tailedness.

steps.slogan: Bound the supremum ratio recursively: $\alpha_{n+1} \le 1 + A + (1+\varepsilon)\alpha_n$.
steps.detail: For $x \le T$ use $\bar F(x) \ge \bar F(T)$. For $x > T$ use the case $n = 2$. Solving the recursion gives $\alpha_n \le ((1+A)/\varepsilon)(1+\varepsilon)^n$.

steps.slogan: Collect the four properties of a subexponential law.
steps.detail: Long-tailedness, slow decay, the relation $\bar F^{n*} \sim n\bar F$ and Kesten's bound together let limits pass through sums with a random number of terms.

new_concepts.name: heavy-tailed distribution
new_concepts.reminder: A heavy-tailed distribution has a right tail that no exponential bound $Ce^{-\varepsilon x}$ controls.
new_concepts.definition: A [random variable](c:random-variable) $X$, or its law, is heavy-tailed (to the right) when $E[e^{\varepsilon X}]=\infty$ for every $\varepsilon>0$, so its [moment generating function](c:moment-generating-function) is infinite on $(0,\infty)$. Equivalently, $\limsup_{x\to\infty}e^{\varepsilon x}P(X>x)=\infty$ for every $\varepsilon>0$.

new_concepts.name: subexponential distribution
new_concepts.reminder: For a subexponential distribution, a sum of independent copies is large mainly because one summand is large.
new_concepts.definition: A [distribution function](c:distribution-function) $F$ on $[0,\infty)$ with $F(x)<1$ for all $x$ is subexponential when $\overline{F^{*2}}(x)/\overline F(x)\to2$ as $x\to\infty$, where $\overline F=1-F$ and $F^{*2}$ is the [convolution](c:convolution) of $F$ with itself. Then, for [iid random variables](c:iid-random-variables) $X_i$ with distribution function $F$ and every $n\ge2$, $P(X_1+\dots+X_n>x)\sim nP(X_1>x)\sim P(\max_{i\le n}X_i>x)$ as $x\to\infty$.

statement: If iid non-negative random variables have a [regularly varying](c:regularly-varying-function) tail, then the sum of $n$ of them exceeds a high level about as often as the largest one does, so their law is [subexponential](c:subexponential-distribution).

hypotheses.text: $X_1, X_2, \dots$ are [independent](c:independent-random-variables) copies of a non-negative random variable $X$.
$\bar F(x) = P(X > x) > 0$ for all $x$, and $\bar F$ is [regularly varying](c:regularly-varying-function) with index $-\alpha$, $\alpha \ge 0$.

conclusion: For every $n \ge 2$, $P(X_1 + \dots + X_n > x)$ is [asymptotically equivalent](c:asymptotic) to $n\bar F(x)$ and to $P(\max_i X_i > x)$ as $x \to \infty$.

proofs.name: Covering by one big jump or two moderate jumps
proofs.slogan: A large sum needs one very large term or two moderately large terms, and the second case is negligible.
proofs.scope: The whole statement, for every $\alpha \ge 0$ and $n \ge 2$.

roles.why: Independence turns the probability of two large terms into a product of two tails.
Regular variation compares the tail at $(1-\delta)x$ and at $\eta$ with the tail at $x$.

steps.slogan: If the sum is large, then one term is very large or two terms are moderately large.
steps.detail: With $\eta = \delta x/(n-1)$: if no term exceeds $(1-\delta)x$ and at most one term exceeds $\eta$, then the sum is at most $(1-\delta)x + (n-1)\eta = x$.

steps.slogan: Apply the union bound and let the shrink factor go to zero.
steps.detail: $P(S_n > x) \le n\bar F((1-\delta)x) + \binom{n}{2}\bar F(\eta)^2$. After division by $n\bar F(x)$, the first term tends to $(1-\delta)^{-\alpha}$ and the second tends to $0$. Then let $\delta \downarrow 0$.

steps.slogan: Bound the sum from below by the union of single large terms, with a Bonferroni correction.
steps.detail: Since the terms are non-negative, $P(S_n > x) \ge P(\max_i X_i > x) \ge n\bar F(x) - \binom{n}{2}\bar F(x)^2$. The correction is $o(\bar F(x))$ because $\bar F(x) \to 0$.

steps.slogan: Squeeze the sum and the maximum between the two bounds.
steps.detail: Both $P(S_n > x)$ and $P(\max_i X_i > x)$ lie between bounds that are asymptotically equivalent to $n\bar F(x)$. This is the definition of a [subexponential distribution](c:subexponential-distribution).

concepts.c:regularly-varying-function: The tail is the regularly varying function that controls the error terms.
concepts.c:subexponential-distribution: The conclusion is the defining property of a subexponential distribution.
concepts.c:independent-random-variables: Independence makes the probability of two large terms the square of a tail.
concepts.c:asymptotic: The conclusion is an asymptotic equivalence of tails.

hypotheses.text: $X_1, X_2, \dots$ are [independent](c:independent-random-variables) with common distribution function $F$.
$\bar F(x) = x^{-\alpha}L(x)$ for $x > 0$, with $\alpha > 0$ and $L$ [slowly varying](c:slowly-varying-function).
$k = k(n) \to \infty$ and $k/n \to 0$.

conclusion: $H_{k,n} = \frac1k\sum_{j=1}^{k}(\ln X_{j,n} - \ln X_{k+1,n}) \to 1/\alpha$ and $\hat\alpha_n = 1/H_{k,n} \to \alpha$ in probability.

proofs.name: Quantile representation, Potter bounds and a law of large numbers
proofs.slogan: Write the data as a regularly varying quantile function of exponential order statistics, compare logs by Potter's bounds, and average the exponential spacings.
proofs.scope: The iid case, every $\alpha > 0$ and every admissible $k(n)$.

roles.why: Independence gives the Rényi representation with independent exponential spacings.
Regular variation of the tail makes the quantile function regularly varying with index $1/\alpha$.
$k \to \infty$ drives the law of large numbers, and $k/n \to 0$ pushes the threshold to infinity.

steps.slogan: Represent the order statistics as $U(e^{E_{(j)}})$ with exponential order statistics $E_{(j)}$.
steps.detail: By the Rényi representation the sum $S_k = \sum_{j \le k}(E_{(j)} - E_{(k+1)})$ is a sum of $k$ independent [exponential](c:exponential-distribution) variables. The weak law gives $S_k/k \to 1$.

steps.slogan: The quantile function $U$ is regularly varying with index $1/\alpha$.
steps.detail: First $y\bar F(U(y)) \to 1$. Then $\lambda y \bar F((1 \pm \eta)\lambda^{1/\alpha}U(y)) \to (1 \pm \eta)^{-\alpha}$ traps $U(\lambda y)$ between $(1 \mp \eta)\lambda^{1/\alpha}U(y)$.

steps.slogan: The threshold $E_{(k+1)}$ tends to infinity in probability.
steps.detail: $E_{(k+1)} \le M$ means that a binomial count with mean $ne^{-M}$ is at most $k = o(n)$. Chebyshev's bound through Markov's inequality makes this unlikely.

steps.slogan: Potter's bounds make each log-ratio equal to $\frac1\alpha(E_{(j)} - E_{(k+1)})$ up to a relative error $\delta$.
steps.detail: On the event that the threshold is large, $|H_{k,n} - S_k/(\alpha k)| \le \delta(S_k/k + 1)$.

steps.slogan: Combine the three limits and invert.
steps.detail: The error bound, $S_k/k \to 1$ and the large threshold give $H_{k,n} \to 1/\alpha$ [in probability](c:convergence-in-probability). The continuous mapping theorem gives $\hat\alpha_n \to \alpha$.

new_concepts.name: exponential distribution
new_concepts.reminder: The exponential distribution with rate $\lambda$ has density $\lambda e^{-\lambda x}$ on $[0,\infty)$ and no memory.
new_concepts.definition: For $\lambda>0$, the exponential distribution with rate $\lambda$ is the law on $[0,\infty)$ with [probability density function](c:probability-density-function) $\lambda e^{-\lambda x}$, so $P(X>x)=e^{-\lambda x}$ and $E[X]=1/\lambda$. new_concepts.reminder: A slowly varying function $L$ satisfies $L(\lambda x)/L(x)\to1$ as $x\to\infty$ for every $\lambda>0$.
new_concepts.definition: A positive [measurable function](c:measurable-function) $L$ on $(0,\infty)$ is slowly varying at infinity when $\lim_{x\to\infty}L(\lambda x)/L(x)=1$ for every $\lambda>0$. Equivalently, $L$ is a [regularly varying function](c:regularly-varying-function) of index $0$. Such an $L$ changes more slowly than every power: $x^{-\varepsilon}L(x)\to0$ and $x^{\varepsilon}L(x)\to\infty$ for every $\varepsilon>0$.

statement: A [distribution function](c:distribution-function) $F$ lies in the [domain of attraction](c:max-domain-of-attraction) of the [Fréchet law](c:frechet-distribution) $\Phi_\alpha(x) = e^{-x^{-\alpha}}$ if and only if its tail $1-F$ is [regularly varying](c:regularly-varying-function) with index $-\alpha$, and then $F^n(U(n)x) \to \Phi_\alpha(x)$.

hypotheses.text: $F$ is a [distribution function](c:distribution-function) with right endpoint $x_F = \sup\{x : F(x) < 1\}$ and tail quantile function $U(t) = \inf\{x : 1 - F(x) \le 1/t\}$.
$\alpha > 0$ is fixed, and $\Phi_\alpha(x) = e^{-x^{-\alpha}}$ for $x > 0$, $\Phi_\alpha(x) = 0$ for $x \le 0$.

conclusion: $F^n(a_n x + b_n) \to \Phi_\alpha(x)$ for some $a_n > 0$ and $b_n$ if and only if $x_F = \infty$ and $\frac{1-F(tx)}{1-F(t)} \to x^{-\alpha}$ for all $x > 0$. Then $a_n = U(n)$ and $b_n = 0$ work.

proofs.name: Poisson criterion and tail inversion
proofs.slogan: Translate maxima into mean numbers of exceedances, then invert the tail through its quantile function.
proofs.scope: Both directions of the equivalence for every $\alpha > 0$, with the norming $a_n = U(n)$, $b_n = 0$.

roles.why: Right continuity of $F$ gives the switching rule $U(t) \le x \iff 1-F(x) \le 1/t$, which every inversion step uses.
The index fixes the target $x^{-\alpha}$ of the mean number of exceedances and the power $y^{1/\alpha}$ of the inverted limit.

steps.slogan: With $a_n = U(n)$, regular variation makes $n(1-F(a_n x))$ tend to $x^{-\alpha}$.
steps.detail: From $1-F(a_n) \le 1/n < 1-F((1-\varepsilon)a_n)$ and regular variation, $n(1-F(a_n)) \to 1$, so $n(1-F(a_n x)) \to x^{-\alpha}$ and the Poisson criterion gives $F^n(a_n x) \to \Phi_\alpha(x)$.

steps.slogan: Invert the limit of the tail to get $\frac{U(ty) - b(t)}{a(t)} \to y^{1/\alpha}$.
steps.detail: The Poisson criterion gives $n(1-F(a_n x + b_n)) \to x^{-\alpha}$. Comparing with $1/y$ at $x = y^{1/\alpha} \pm \varepsilon$ traps $U(ny)$, and the [monotone](c:monotone-function) $U$ extends the limit from integers to real $t$.

steps.slogan: Two levels give the ratio $a(ty)/a(t) \to y^{1/\alpha}$ of the scales.
steps.detail: Write $U(2ty) - U(ty)$ once with the scale $a(t)$ and once with $a(ty)$. The two expansions give $a(ty)/a(t) \to y^{1/\alpha}$, and in particular $a(2s)/a(s) \to 2^{1/\alpha} > 1$.

steps.slogan: A geometric dyadic sum shows $U(t)/a(t) \to 1$, so the centring is negligible.
steps.detail: Telescope $U(t) - U(2^{-K}t)$ over dyadic scales. Each term is dominated by $C\rho^{-j}$ with $\rho > 1$, so Tannery's theorem gives the limit $\sum_{j \ge 1}(2^{1/\alpha}-1)2^{-j/\alpha} = 1$. Hence $b(t)/a(t) \to 0$, $U$ is unbounded and $x_F = \infty$.

steps.slogan: Put $t = 1/(1-F(x))$ and transfer the scaling of $U$ back to the tail.
steps.detail: Then $U(t) \le x < U(t(1+\delta))$, and $U(tc)/U(t) \to c^{1/\alpha}$ compares $\lambda x$ with $U(tc)$ for $c$ near $\lambda^\alpha$. This gives $\frac{1-F(\lambda x)}{1-F(x)} \to \lambda^{-\alpha}$.

steps.slogan: The two directions together give the equivalence and the norming $a_n = U(n)$.
steps.detail: Sufficiency gives the limit with $b_n = 0$ and $a_n = U(n)$. Necessity gives $x_F = \infty$ and the regular variation of the tail with index $-\alpha$.

new_concepts.name: extreme value distribution
new_concepts.reminder: An extreme value distribution is a nondegenerate limit law of affinely normalized maxima of iid random variables.
new_concepts.definition: A nondegenerate [distribution function](c:distribution-function) $G$ is an extreme value distribution when there are [iid random variables](c:iid-random-variables) $X_1,X_2,\dots$ and constants $a_n>0$ and $b_n$ such that $(\max_{i\le n}X_i-b_n)/a_n$ [converges in distribution](c:convergence-in-distribution) to $G$. By the Fisher–Tippett–Gnedenko theorem, these are exactly the laws $G_\xi(ax+b)$ with $a>0$, $b\in\mathbb{R}$, $G_\xi(x)=\exp(-(1+\xi x)^{-1/\xi})$ where $1+\xi x>0$, and $G_0(x)=\exp(-e^{-x})$. The shapes $\xi=0$, $\xi>0$ and $\xi<0$ give the Gumbel, Fréchet and reversed Weibull types.

new_concepts.name: Frechet distribution
new_concepts.reminder: The Fréchet distribution with index $\alpha$ has distribution function $\exp(-x^{-\alpha})$ for $x>0$ and governs maxima of heavy tails.
new_concepts.definition: For $\alpha>0$, the Fréchet distribution $\Phi_\alpha$ is the law on $(0,\infty)$ with [distribution function](c:distribution-function) $\Phi_\alpha(x)=\exp(-x^{-\alpha})$ for $x>0$ and $\Phi_\alpha(x)=0$ for $x\le0$. It is the [extreme value distribution](c:extreme-value-distribution) with shape $\xi=1/\alpha$, up to an affine change of variable. Its moment $E[X^p]=\Gamma(1-p/\alpha)$ is finite exactly when $p<\alpha$.

new_concepts.name: maximum domain of attraction
new_concepts.reminder: The maximum domain of attraction of $G$ collects the laws whose normalized sample maxima converge in distribution to $G$.
new_concepts.definition: Let $G$ be an [extreme value distribution](c:extreme-value-distribution). A [distribution function](c:distribution-function) $F$ lies in the maximum domain of attraction of $G$, written $F\in\mathrm{MDA}(G)$, when for [iid random variables](c:iid-random-variables) $X_1,X_2,\dots$ with distribution function $F$ and $M_n=\max(X_1,\dots,X_n)$ there are constants $a_n>0$ and $b_n\in\mathbb{R}$ with $(M_n-b_n)/a_n\to G$ in distribution. Equivalently, $F(a_nx+b_n)^n\to G(x)$ for every real $x$.

new_concepts.name: regularly varying function
new_concepts.reminder: A regularly varying function grows like a power $x^\rho$ times a slowly varying factor at infinity.
new_concepts.definition: A positive [measurable function](c:measurable-function) $f$ on $(0,\infty)$ is regularly varying at infinity with index $\rho\in\mathbb{R}$ when $\lim_{x\to\infty}f(\lambda x)/f(x)=\lambda^\rho$ for every $\lambda>0$. Every such $f$ has the form $f(x)=x^\rho L(x)$, where $L$ is a [slowly varying function](c:slowly-varying-function).

statement: A [distribution function](c:distribution-function) $F$ lies in the [domain of attraction](c:max-domain-of-attraction) of the Weibull [extreme value law](c:extreme-value-distribution) $\Psi_\alpha(x) = e^{-(-x)^\alpha}$ if and only if its right endpoint $x_F$ is finite and $1-F(x_F - h)$ is [regularly varying](c:regularly-varying-function) at $h = 0$ with index $\alpha$.

hypotheses.text: $F$ is a [distribution function](c:distribution-function) with right endpoint $x_F = \sup\{x : F(x) < 1\}$ and tail quantile function $U(t) = \inf\{x : 1-F(x) \le 1/t\}$.
$\alpha > 0$ is fixed, and $\Psi_\alpha(x) = e^{-(-x)^\alpha}$ for $x < 0$, $\Psi_\alpha(x) = 1$ for $x \ge 0$.

conclusion: $F^n(a_n x + b_n) \to \Psi_\alpha(x)$ for some $a_n > 0$ and $b_n$ if and only if $x_F < \infty$ and $\frac{1-F(x_F - xh)}{1-F(x_F - h)} \to x^\alpha$ as $h \downarrow 0$ for all $x > 0$. Then $b_n = x_F$ and $a_n = x_F - U(n)$ work.

proofs.name: Inversion of the endpoint
proofs.slogan: Send the finite endpoint to infinity with $y \mapsto x_F - 1/y$ and use the Fréchet criterion.
proofs.scope: Both directions of the equivalence for every $\alpha > 0$, with the norming $a_n = x_F - U(n)$, $b_n = x_F$.

roles.why: The endpoint and the tail quantile function define the transformed law $F^*$ and the norming constants.
The index fixes the exponent $x^\alpha$ near the endpoint, which becomes the Fréchet index of $F^*$ at infinity.

steps.slogan: The map $y \mapsto x_F - 1/y$ turns the endpoint condition into regular variation at infinity.
steps.detail: Put $F^*(y) = F(x_F - 1/y)$ for $y > 0$. With $h = 1/t$ and $x = 1/y$, $\frac{1-F^*(ty)}{1-F^*(t)} = \frac{1-F(x_F - xh)}{1-F(x_F - h)}$, so the condition says that $1-F^*$ is regularly varying with index $-\alpha$.

steps.slogan: Apply the Fréchet criterion to $F^*$ and map the limit back.
steps.detail: The Fréchet criterion gives $F^{*n}(c_n y) \to \Phi_\alpha(y)$ with $c_n = 1/(x_F - U(n))$. Substituting $y = -1/x$ gives $F^n(x_F + x/c_n) \to e^{-(-x)^\alpha}$ for $x < 0$.

steps.slogan: Invert the limit to get $\frac{U(ty) - b(t)}{a(t)} \to -y^{-1/\alpha}$.
steps.detail: The Poisson criterion gives $n(1-F(a_n x + b_n)) \to (-x)^\alpha$ for $x < 0$. Comparing with $1/y$ traps $U(ny)$, and the [monotone](c:monotone-function) $U$ extends the limit to real $t$.

steps.slogan: Shrinking scales make the dyadic increments of $U$ summable, so the endpoint is finite.
steps.detail: Since $a(2s)/a(s) \to 2^{-1/\alpha} < 1$, the increments $U(2^{j+1}t) - U(2^j t)$ decay geometrically. So $x_F = \lim U(t) < \infty$, and Tannery's theorem gives $(x_F - U(t))/a(t) \to 1$ and $(x_F - b_n)/a_n \to 0$.

steps.slogan: Recentre at $x_F$, check that $F^*$ is in the Fréchet domain and read off the tail.
steps.detail: There is no atom at $x_F$, and $(x_F - b_n)/a_n \to 0$ gives $F^{*n}(y/a_n) \to \Phi_\alpha(y)$. The Fréchet criterion makes $1-F^*$ regularly varying, which is the endpoint condition.

steps.slogan: The two directions together give the equivalence and the norming at the endpoint.
steps.detail: Sufficiency gives the Weibull limit with $b_n = x_F$ and $a_n = x_F - U(n)$. Necessity gives a finite endpoint and the regular variation of $1-F(x_F - h)$ with index $\alpha$.

proofs.name: De Haan's mean excess argument
proofs.slogan: Smooth the law, read the auxiliary function off the integrated quantile function, and transfer it back.
proofs.scope: Outline of de Haan's proof of Theorem 2.5.1 and Corollary 2.5.1 (1970). Mejzler's theorem, Gnedenko's theorem and the smoothing lemma are taken from the source.

roles.why: The tail and its quantile function give the centring $U(n)$ and the mean excess function, and the smoothing step replaces $F$ by a continuous law with the same tail.
The Gumbel limit forces the logarithmic scaling of the quantile function, which is what makes the integral auxiliary function work.

steps.slogan: An auxiliary function gives $n(1-F(b_n + x g(b_n))) \to e^{-x}$ and so the Gumbel limit.
steps.detail: With $b_n = U(n)$, the bounds $1-F(b_n) \le 1/n \le 1-F(b_n - \varepsilon g(b_n))$ give $n(1-F(b_n)) \to 1$, and the Poisson criterion gives $F^n(g(b_n)x + b_n) \to \Lambda(x)$.

steps.slogan: Gumbel maxima force logarithmic ratios of quantile increments.
steps.detail: Convergence of types gives $s(1-F(a(s)x+b(s))) \to e^{-x}$ with $b(s) = U(s)$. Mejzler's theorem gives $\frac{U(tx)-U(t)}{U(ty)-U(t)} \to \frac{\log x}{\log y}$ for the [generalized inverse](c:generalized-inverse) $U$ as $t \to \infty$.

steps.slogan: Replace $F$ by a continuous strictly increasing $G$ with an equivalent tail.
steps.detail: Linear interpolation across the jumps and flat parts of $F$ gives $G$ with $\frac{1-F(x)}{1-G(x)} \to 1$ as $x \uparrow x_F$, and $G$ is again in the Gumbel domain.

steps.slogan: The averaged quantile function minus the quantile is an auxiliary function.
steps.detail: For $G$, the logarithmic ratio limit and de Haan's Theorem 1.4.3 allow the scale $a(s) = s\int_0^{1/s} V_G(p)\,dp - V_G(1/s)$, where $V_G(p) = \inf\{y : 1-G(y) \le p\}$, with the finite integral.

steps.slogan: At $s = 1/(1-G(t))$ the averaged quantile scale equals the mean excess of $G$.
steps.detail: Since $V_G(p) > y$ exactly when $p < 1-G(y)$, Tonelli's theorem gives $\int_0^{1-G(t)}(V_G(p) - t)\,dp = \int_t^{x_F}(1-G(y))\,dy$. So $a(s)$ is the mean excess $g(t)$ of $G$.

steps.slogan: Tail equivalence carries the mean excess function and the norming back to $F$.
steps.detail: Tail integrals of equivalent tails are equivalent, so $f/g \to 1$, and an asymptotically equal auxiliary function may replace $g$. Then $b_n = U(n)$ and $a_n = f(b_n)$ give the limit, as in the sufficiency step.

statement: If the [density](c:probability-density-function) $f$ of $F$ is positive and differentiable near $x_F$ and $h = (1-F)/f$ satisfies $h' \to 0$, then $F$ is in the [domain of attraction](c:max-domain-of-attraction) of the [Gumbel law](c:gumbel-distribution), with $b_n = U(n)$ and $a_n = h(b_n)$.

hypotheses.text: $F$ is a [distribution function](c:distribution-function) with a [density](c:probability-density-function) $f$ that is positive and differentiable on $(z_0, x_F)$, where $x_F \le \infty$ is the right endpoint.
The reciprocal hazard rate $h = (1-F)/f$ satisfies $h'(x) \to 0$ as $x \uparrow x_F$.

conclusion: $\frac{1-F(t+xh(t))}{1-F(t)} \to e^{-x}$ as $t \uparrow x_F$, and $F^n(h(b_n)x + b_n) \to \exp(-e^{-x})$ for every real $x$, with $b_n = \inf\{x : 1-F(x) \le 1/n\}$.

proofs.name: Hazard representation
proofs.slogan: Write the tail as the exponential of minus the integrated hazard, and use that $h$ is almost constant on the scale $h(t)$.
proofs.scope: Both conclusions, for finite and infinite right endpoints.

roles.why: A positive differentiable density makes $\log(1-F)$ differentiable with derivative $-1/h$, which gives the exponential representation of the tail.
The condition $h' \to 0$ makes $h$ small compared with the distance to the endpoint and almost constant on intervals of length $h(t)$.

steps.slogan: The tail is the exponential of minus the integral of the hazard rate $1/h$.
steps.detail: Since $(\log(1-F))' = -f/(1-F) = -1/h$, the fundamental theorem of calculus gives $1-F(x) = (1-F(z))\exp(-\int_z^x ds/h(s))$, and the integral diverges at $x_F$ because $1-F(x) \to 0$.

steps.slogan: The scale $h(t)$ is small compared with $t$, or with the distance $x_F - t$.
steps.detail: Integrating $|h'| \le \varepsilon$ gives $h(t)/t \to 0$ if $x_F = \infty$. If $x_F < \infty$, the divergent integral forces $h(x_F-) = 0$, and then $h(t)/(x_F - t) \to 0$.

steps.slogan: On the interval from $t$ to $t + xh(t)$ the function $h$ hardly changes.
steps.detail: The mean value theorem gives $|h(s) - h(t)| \le \varepsilon |x| h(t)$ on that interval, so $h(s)/h(t) \to 1$ uniformly there as $t \uparrow x_F$.

steps.slogan: Rescale the hazard integral to get the limit $e^{-x}$ of the tail ratio.
steps.detail: With $s = t + uh(t)$, $\int_t^{t+xh(t)} \frac{ds}{h(s)} = \int_0^x \frac{h(t)}{h(t+uh(t))}\,du \to x$. So $\frac{1-F(t+xh(t))}{1-F(t)} \to e^{-x}$.

steps.slogan: Put $t = b_n$ and apply the Poisson criterion.
steps.detail: The continuous tail gives $1-F(b_n) = 1/n$, so $n(1-F(h(b_n)x + b_n)) \to e^{-x}$, and the Poisson criterion gives the [Gumbel](c:gumbel-distribution) limit.

new_concepts.name: extreme value distribution
new_concepts.reminder: An extreme value distribution is a nondegenerate limit law of affinely normalized maxima of iid random variables.
new_concepts.definition: A nondegenerate [distribution function](c:distribution-function) $G$ is an extreme value distribution when there are [iid random variables](c:iid-random-variables) $X_1,X_2,\dots$ and constants $a_n>0$ and $b_n$ such that $(\max_{i\le n}X_i-b_n)/a_n$ [converges in distribution](c:convergence-in-distribution) to $G$. By the Fisher–Tippett–Gnedenko theorem, these are exactly the laws $G_\xi(ax+b)$ with $a>0$, $b\in\mathbb{R}$, $G_\xi(x)=\exp(-(1+\xi x)^{-1/\xi})$ where $1+\xi x>0$, and $G_0(x)=\exp(-e^{-x})$. The shapes $\xi=0$, $\xi>0$ and $\xi<0$ give the Gumbel, Fréchet and reversed Weibull types.

new_concepts.name: Gumbel distribution
new_concepts.reminder: The Gumbel distribution has distribution function $\exp(-e^{-x})$ on $\mathbb{R}$ and is the limit law of many normalized maxima.
new_concepts.definition: The standard Gumbel distribution is the probability law on $\mathbb{R}$ with [distribution function](c:distribution-function) $\Lambda(x)=\exp(-e^{-x})$. Its density is $e^{-x}\exp(-e^{-x})$, its mean is the Euler–Mascheroni constant $\gamma\approx0.5772$, and its variance is $\pi^2/6$. It is the [extreme value distribution](c:extreme-value-distribution) with shape $\xi=0$.

new_concepts.name: maximum domain of attraction
new_concepts.reminder: The maximum domain of attraction of $G$ collects the laws whose normalized sample maxima converge in distribution to $G$.
new_concepts.definition: Let $G$ be an [extreme value distribution](c:extreme-value-distribution). A [distribution function](c:distribution-function) $F$ lies in the maximum domain of attraction of $G$, written $F\in\mathrm{MDA}(G)$, when for [iid random variables](c:iid-random-variables) $X_1,X_2,\dots$ with distribution function $F$ and $M_n=\max(X_1,\dots,X_n)$ there are constants $a_n>0$ and $b_n\in\mathbb{R}$ with $(M_n-b_n)/a_n\to G$ in distribution. Equivalently, $F(a_nx+b_n)^n\to G(x)$ for every real $x$.

statement: For [iid](c:iid-random-variables) random variables with [distribution function](c:distribution-function) $F$, real levels $u_n$ and $\tau \in [0,\infty]$, the maximum satisfies $P(M_n \le u_n) \to e^{-\tau}$ if and only if $n(1-F(u_n)) \to \tau$, the mean of the [binomial](c:binomial-distribution) number of exceedances.

hypotheses.text: The variables $X_1, X_2, \dots$ are [independent and identically distributed](c:iid-random-variables) with [distribution function](c:distribution-function) $F$, and $M_n = \max(X_1, \dots, X_n)$.
The levels $u_n$ are real numbers and $\tau \in [0,\infty]$, with the convention $e^{-\infty} = 0$.

conclusion: $P(M_n \le u_n) \to e^{-\tau}$ if and only if $n(1-F(u_n)) \to \tau$. The limit $e^{-\tau}$ is the probability that a [Poisson](c:poisson-distribution) variable with mean $\tau$ is zero.

proofs.name: Product formula and subsequences
proofs.slogan: Write the probability as $(1-p_n)^n$, compare $\log(1-p)$ with $-p$, and get the converse from convergent subsequences.
proofs.scope: The whole criterion, in both directions and for every $\tau \in [0,\infty]$, including $\tau = 0$ and $\tau = \infty$.

roles.why: Independence turns the probability that no variable exceeds $u_n$ into the power $(1-p_n)^n$.
The value $\tau$ may be finite or infinite, so the proof treats both kinds of subsequential limits.

steps.slogan: Write the probability of no exceedance as the power $(1-p_n)^n$.
steps.detail: Independence gives $P(M_n \le u_n) = \prod_{i \le n} P(X_i \le u_n) = (1-p_n)^n$ with $p_n = 1-F(u_n)$. So the claim is that $(1-p_n)^n \to e^{-\tau}$ if and only if $n p_n \to \tau$.

steps.slogan: Bound $\log(1-p)$ between $-p-p^2$ and $-p$ for small $p$.
steps.detail: Convexity of $e^{-p}$ gives $1-p \le e^{-p}$, so $(1-p)^n \le e^{-np}$. For $p \le 1/2$ the series $\log(1-p) = -\sum_k p^k/k$ gives $-p-p^2 \le \log(1-p) \le -p$.

steps.slogan: Along a subsequence with finite limit $\sigma$ of $n p_n$, the power tends to $e^{-\sigma}$.
steps.detail: Then $p_{n_k} \to 0$, and the bounds give $|n_k \log(1-p_{n_k}) + n_k p_{n_k}| \le n_k p_{n_k}^2 \to 0$. So $n_k \log(1-p_{n_k}) \to -\sigma$ and $(1-p_{n_k})^{n_k} \to e^{-\sigma}$.

steps.slogan: Along a subsequence with $n p_n \to \infty$, the power tends to zero.
steps.detail: The bound $(1-p)^n \le e^{-np}$ gives $(1-p_{n_k})^{n_k} \le e^{-n_k p_{n_k}} \to 0$. Together with the finite case and $n_k = k$, this proves that $n p_n \to \tau$ implies $P(M_n \le u_n) \to e^{-\tau}$.

steps.slogan: Prove necessity with a convergent [subsequence](c:subsequence) and the injectivity of $x \mapsto e^{-x}$.
steps.detail: If $n p_n$ does not tend to $\tau$, compactness of $[0,\infty]$ gives a subsequence with $n_k p_{n_k} \to \sigma \ne \tau$. The two previous steps give the limit $e^{-\sigma} \ne e^{-\tau}$ along it, which contradicts the hypothesis.

concepts.c:iid-random-variables: Independence and a common law make the probability a power of one number.
concepts.c:distribution-function: The tail $1-F(u_n)$ of the distribution function is the probability of one exceedance.
concepts.c:binomial-distribution: The number of exceedances of $u_n$ is binomial with mean $n(1-F(u_n))$.
concepts.c:poisson-distribution: The limit $e^{-\tau}$ is the Poisson probability of no exceedance.
concepts.c:subsequence: Convergent subsequences in $[0,\infty]$ give the converse direction.

statement: For [iid](c:iid-random-variables) variables and levels $u_n$ with $n(1-F(u_n)) \to \tau \in (0,\infty)$, the [point process](c:point-process) of rescaled exceedance times $\{i/n : X_i > u_n\}$ converges to the homogeneous [Poisson process](c:poisson-process) with intensity $\tau$, in [Laplace functionals](c:laplace-transform) and in joint counts on disjoint intervals.

hypotheses.text: The variables $X_1, X_2, \dots$ are [independent and identically distributed](c:iid-random-variables) with distribution function $F$.
The levels satisfy $n(1-F(u_n)) \to \tau$ for a fixed $\tau \in (0,\infty)$.

conclusion: $\mathbb{E}\exp(-\sum_{i \ge 1} f(i/n)\mathbf{1}\{X_i > u_n\}) \to \exp(-\tau\int_0^\infty (1-e^{-f(x)})\,dx)$ for continuous compactly supported $f \ge 0$, and the counts on disjoint bounded intervals converge to independent [Poisson](c:poisson-distribution) variables with means $\tau|I_j|$.

proofs.name: Laplace functionals and binomial counts
proofs.slogan: Independence factorizes the Laplace functional into a product whose logarithm is a Riemann sum, and the interval counts are independent binomials with Poisson limits.
proofs.scope: Parts (a) and (b). The equivalence of Laplace functional convergence with weak convergence in the vague topology is cited, not proved.

roles.why: Independence of the exceedance indicators factorizes the Laplace functional and makes counts on disjoint intervals independent.
The mean number of exceedances per unit time tends to $\tau$, which fixes the Poisson intensity.

steps.slogan: Factorize the Laplace functional over the independent exceedance indicators.
steps.detail: With $p_n = 1-F(u_n)$ and $g = 1-e^{-f}$, independence gives $\mathbb{E}\exp(-\sum_i f(i/n)B_i) = \prod_{i \le nL}(1-p_n g(i/n))$ when $f$ vanishes outside $[0,L]$.

steps.slogan: Take logarithms and recognize a [Riemann sum](c:riemann-integral) of $1-e^{-f}$.
steps.detail: The bound $|\log(1-y)+y| \le y^2$ for $y \le 1/2$ gives an error at most $p_n^2(nL+1) \to 0$, and $p_n\sum_i g(i/n) = (np_n)\cdot\frac1n\sum_i g(i/n) \to \tau\int_0^\infty g(x)\,dx$.

steps.slogan: Show that counts on disjoint intervals are independent [binomial](c:binomial-distribution) variables.
steps.detail: An interval of length $\ell$ contains $m_n$ grid points $i/n$ with $|m_n - n\ell| \le 1$, so its count is binomial with parameters $m_n$ and $p_n$, and disjoint intervals use disjoint independent indicators.

steps.slogan: Pass each binomial count to its Poisson limit and multiply the limits.
steps.detail: Since $m_n p_n \to \tau\ell$, the binomial mass function converges to the Poisson mass function with mean $\tau\ell$, and the product over disjoint intervals converges to the joint law of independent Poisson counts.

steps.slogan: Identify both limits with those of the homogeneous [Poisson process](c:poisson-process).
steps.detail: The limit $\exp(-\tau\int(1-e^{-f}))$ is the Laplace functional of the Poisson process with intensity $\tau$, and its counts on disjoint intervals are independent Poisson variables, so both limits are those of this process.

concepts.c:iid-random-variables: Independence makes the exceedance indicators independent Bernoulli variables.
concepts.c:point-process: The rescaled exceedance times form a random point process on the half-line.
concepts.c:poisson-process: The homogeneous Poisson process with intensity $\tau$ is the limit object.
concepts.c:laplace-transform: Laplace functionals characterize the law of a point process and its convergence.
concepts.c:poisson-distribution: Counts of the limit process on intervals have Poisson laws.
concepts.c:binomial-distribution: Counts of exceedances on intervals have binomial laws before the limit.
concepts.c:riemann-integral: The logarithm of the Laplace functional is a Riemann sum that converges to an integral.

new_concepts.name: point process
new_concepts.reminder: A point process is a random locally finite set of points, described by the random counts it puts in sets.
new_concepts.definition: Let $E$ be a locally compact Hausdorff space with a countable base, and let $M_p(E)$ be the set of [Radon measures](c:radon-measure) on $E$ with values in $\{0,1,2,\dots,\infty\}$, which are the locally finite sums of [Dirac measures](c:dirac-measure). A point process on $E$ is a [random variable](c:random-variable) $N$ with values in $M_p(E)$, where $M_p(E)$ has the sigma-algebra generated by the maps $\mu\mapsto\mu(B)$ for Borel sets $B$. Each count $N(B)$ is then a random variable, and it is finite when $B$ is relatively compact.

statement: For [iid](c:iid-random-variables) variables and levels $u_n$ with $n(1-F(u_n)) \to \tau < \infty$, the $k$-th largest [order statistic](c:order-statistic) satisfies $P(M_n^{(k)} \le u_n) \to e^{-\tau}\sum_{s<k} \tau^s/s!$. The converse holds, and a limit law $G$ of the normalized maximum gives the limit $G(x)\sum_{s<k}(-\log G(x))^s/s!$.

hypotheses.text: The variables $X_1, X_2, \dots$ are [independent and identically distributed](c:iid-random-variables) with distribution function $F$.
The integer $k \ge 1$ is fixed and $u_n$ are real levels. For the last part, $P(a_n(M_n - b_n) \le x) \to G(x)$ at the point $x$.

conclusion: $P(M_n^{(k)} \le u_n) \to e^{-\tau}\sum_{s=0}^{k-1}\tau^s/s!$ if and only if $n(1-F(u_n)) \to \tau$, and $P(a_n(M_n^{(k)} - b_n) \le x) \to G(x)\sum_{s=0}^{k-1}(-\log G(x))^s/s!$.

proofs.name: Count the exceedances
proofs.slogan: The $k$-th largest value is below $u_n$ exactly when fewer than $k$ values exceed $u_n$, and that binomial count has a Poisson limit.
proofs.scope: All three parts, for every fixed $k \ge 1$. Part (a) needs a finite limit $\tau$, and part (b) allows $\tau = \infty$.

roles.why: Independence makes the number of exceedances [binomial](c:binomial-distribution) with success probability $1-F(u_n)$.
The levels fix the mean $n(1-F(u_n))$ of the count, and the limit of the maximum fixes the level $b_n + x/a_n$.

steps.slogan: Turn the event for the $k$-th largest value into a count of exceedances.
steps.detail: At least $k$ values exceed $u$ exactly when the $k$-th largest value exceeds $u$, so $\{M_n^{(k)} \le u\} = \{S_n(u) < k\}$, and $S_n(u_n)$ is binomial with parameters $n$ and $p_n = 1-F(u_n)$.

steps.slogan: Expand the binomial probabilities and pass to the [Poisson](c:poisson-distribution) limit.
steps.detail: Write $P(S_n = s) = \prod_{j<s}(1-j/n)\,(np_n)^s/s!\,(1-p_n)^n(1-p_n)^{-s}$. With $np_n \to \tau$ and $(1-p_n)^n \to e^{-\tau}$ this tends to $e^{-\tau}\tau^s/s!$, and the sum over $s < k$ gives part (a).

steps.slogan: Show that an infinite mean number of exceedances forces at least $k$ of them.
steps.detail: If $np_n \to \infty$, Chebyshev's inequality gives $P(S_n < k) \le np_n/(np_n-k)^2 \to 0$, which is the limit for $\tau = \infty$.

steps.slogan: Get the converse from the strict decrease of the Poisson tail in $\tau$.
steps.detail: The function $Q_k(\tau) = e^{-\tau}\sum_{s<k}\tau^s/s!$ has derivative $-e^{-\tau}\tau^{k-1}/(k-1)! < 0$, so it is injective on $[0,\infty]$. A subsequence with a different limit $\sigma$ of $np_n$ would give the different limit $Q_k(\sigma)$.

steps.slogan: Transfer a limit law of the maximum to the $k$-th largest value.
steps.detail: Put $u_n = b_n + x/a_n$ and $\tau = -\log G(x)$. The converse with $k = 1$ gives $n(1-F(u_n)) \to \tau$, and part (a) or the Chebyshev step gives the limit $G(x)\sum_{s<k}(-\log G(x))^s/s!$ for the [extreme value](c:extreme-value-distribution) law $G$.

concepts.c:order-statistic: The $k$-th largest value is the order statistic whose limit law the theorem gives.
concepts.c:binomial-distribution: The number of exceedances of $u_n$ is binomial with parameters $n$ and $1-F(u_n)$.
concepts.c:poisson-distribution: The binomial count converges to a Poisson law with mean $\tau$.
concepts.c:extreme-value-distribution: The limit law $G$ of the normalized maximum is an extreme value distribution.

statement: The [order statistics](c:order-statistic) $Y_{(1)} \ge \dots \ge Y_{(n)}$ of $n$ [iid](c:iid-random-variables) [standard exponential](c:exponential-distribution) variables have the joint law of $(\sum_{k=i}^n E_k/k)_{i \le n}$ with $E_k$ iid standard exponential, and the order statistics of a sample from any $F$ have the law of $(U(e^{Y_{(i)}}))_{i \le n}$.

hypotheses.text: $Y_1, \dots, Y_n$ are [independent](c:iid-random-variables) with the [standard exponential law](c:exponential-distribution) $P(Y_j > y) = e^{-y}$.

For the last part, $X_1, \dots, X_n$ are iid with [distribution function](c:distribution-function) $F$, and $U(t) = \inf\{x : F(x) \ge 1 - 1/t\}$ is its [generalized inverse](c:generalized-inverse) tail quantile function.

conclusion: $(Y_{(1)}, \dots, Y_{(n)}) \overset{d}{=} (\sum_{k=i}^n E_k/k)_{i=1}^n$, so the spacings $k(Y_{(k)} - Y_{(k+1)})$ are iid standard exponential, and $(X_{(1)}, \dots, X_{(n)}) \overset{d}{=} (U(e^{Y_{(1)}}), \dots, U(e^{Y_{(n)}}))$.

proofs.name: Density of the spacings and quantile transform
proofs.slogan: Change variables from the ordered exponential sample to its normalized spacings, then push the sample forward by the monotone map $U \circ \exp$.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, for every $n \ge 1$ and every distribution function $F$.

roles.why: The exponential density turns the sum of the ordered values into a sum of weighted spacings with a product density.
The quantile function $U$ maps exponential variables to variables with law $F$ and keeps the order.

steps.slogan: Write the joint density of the ordered exponential sample.
steps.detail: Ties have probability zero, and summing over the $n!$ orderings gives the density $n!\,e^{-\sum_j z_j}$ on $\{0 < z_1 < \dots < z_n\}$ for the increasing order statistics.

steps.slogan: Change variables to the normalized spacings $w_j = (n-j+1)(z_j - z_{j-1})$.
steps.detail: The map is triangular with [Jacobian determinant](c:jacobian-determinant) $n!$ and satisfies $\sum_j z_j = \sum_j w_j$, so the new density is $\prod_j e^{-w_j}$ on $(0,\infty)^n$ and the spacings are iid exponential.

steps.slogan: Invert the spacings to write each order statistic as a weighted sum.
steps.detail: Summing the increments gives $Y_{(i)} = \sum_{k=i}^n E_k/k$ with $E_k = W_{n-k+1}$, and $k(Y_{(k)} - Y_{(k+1)}) = E_k$ for each $k$.

steps.slogan: Show that $U(e^{Y})$ has law $F$ for an exponential variable $Y$.
steps.detail: Right-continuity of $F$ gives $U(t) \le x$ exactly when $F(x) \ge 1 - 1/t$, so $P(U(e^Y) \le x) = P(Y \le -\log(1-F(x))) = F(x)$.

steps.slogan: Use that the non-decreasing map $U \circ \exp$ keeps the order of the sample.
steps.detail: A non-decreasing map sends the $i$-th largest value to the $i$-th largest image, so the order statistics of the transformed sample are $U(e^{Y_{(i)}})$, which proves the last claim.

concepts.c:order-statistic: The theorem describes the joint law of all order statistics of the sample.
concepts.c:iid-random-variables: The sample and the variables $E_k$ are independent with a common law.
concepts.c:exponential-distribution: The exponential law makes the normalized spacings independent and exponential.
concepts.c:distribution-function: Any law $F$ enters through its distribution function and its quantile function.
concepts.c:generalized-inverse: The tail quantile function $U$ is the generalized inverse of $1/(1-F)$.
concepts.c:jacobian-determinant: The determinant $n!$ of the spacing map cancels the factor $n!$ of the ordered density.

source.note: Boucheron and Thomas (arXiv 1207.7209, ECP 2012) state the representation as Theorem 2.5 on p. 4 without proof. These steps give the classical proof by the density of the spacings and the quantile transform.

new_concepts.name: exponential distribution
new_concepts.reminder: The exponential distribution with rate $\lambda$ has density $\lambda e^{-\lambda x}$ on $[0,\infty)$ and no memory.
new_concepts.definition: For $\lambda>0$, the exponential distribution with rate $\lambda$ is the law on $[0,\infty)$ with [probability density function](c:probability-density-function) $\lambda e^{-\lambda x}$, so $P(X>x)=e^{-\lambda x}$ and $E[X]=1/\lambda$. Among laws of positive random variables, it is the only one with the memoryless property $P(X>s+t\mid X>s)=P(X>t)$ for all $s,t\ge0$.

statement: The maximum $M_n$ of $n$ [iid](c:iid-random-variables) [standard normal](c:normal-distribution) variables satisfies $P(a_n(M_n - b_n) \le x) \to \exp(-e^{-x})$, the [Gumbel distribution](c:gumbel-distribution), with $a_n = \sqrt{2\log n}$ and $b_n = a_n - (\log\log n + \log 4\pi)/(2a_n)$.

hypotheses.text: The variables $X_1, X_2, \dots$ are [independent and identically distributed](c:iid-random-variables) with the [standard normal law](c:normal-distribution) $N(0,1)$.
For $n \ge 3$, $a_n = \sqrt{2\log n}$ and $b_n = \sqrt{2\log n} - (\log\log n + \log 4\pi)/(2\sqrt{2\log n})$.

conclusion: $P(a_n(M_n - b_n) \le x) \to \exp(-e^{-x})$ for every real $x$, so the normal law lies in the [Gumbel domain of attraction](c:max-domain-of-attraction).

proofs.name: Mills ratio and the Poisson criterion
proofs.slogan: Estimate the normal tail by $\varphi(u)/u$, choose $u_n$ so that $n$ times the tail tends to $e^{-x}$, and apply the Poisson criterion.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, for every real $x$.

roles.why: The explicit normal density gives the tail estimate and makes the variables independent with one common law.
The constants are chosen so that the logarithm of the mean number of exceedances tends to $-x$.

steps.slogan: Bound the [normal](c:normal-distribution) tail by the Mills ratio estimates.
steps.detail: From $\varphi'(t) = -t\varphi(t)$ one gets $\varphi(u)(1/u - 1/u^3) \le 1 - \Phi(u) \le \varphi(u)/u$ for $u > 0$, by comparing the integrands and integrating an exact derivative.

steps.slogan: Expand $u_n^2$ for the level $u_n = b_n + x/a_n$.
steps.detail: With $L = \log n$ the expansion gives $u_n^2/2 = L - \tfrac12\log L - \tfrac12\log 4\pi + x + o(1)$ and $u_n/a_n \to 1$, because the correction to $b_n$ is small against $a_n$.

steps.slogan: Show that the mean number of exceedances $n(1-\Phi(u_n))$ tends to $e^{-x}$.
steps.detail: In $\log(n\varphi(u_n)/u_n)$ the terms in $\log L$ cancel, and the constants give $\tfrac12\log(4\pi/(2\pi\cdot 2)) = 0$, so the limit is $-x$. The Mills bounds then give $n(1-\Phi(u_n)) \to e^{-x}$.

steps.slogan: Turn the mean number of exceedances into the law of the maximum by the Poisson criterion.
steps.detail: Since $\{a_n(M_n - b_n) \le x\} = \{M_n \le u_n\}$ and $n(1-\Phi(u_n)) \to e^{-x}$, the Poisson criterion for [iid](c:iid-random-variables) maxima gives the [Gumbel](c:gumbel-distribution) limit $\exp(-e^{-x})$.

concepts.c:iid-random-variables: Independence with a common law reduces the maximum to a power of $\Phi$.
concepts.c:normal-distribution: The explicit normal density determines the tail and the constants $a_n$ and $b_n$.
concepts.c:gumbel-distribution: The Gumbel law $\exp(-e^{-x})$ is the limit of the normalized maximum.
concepts.c:max-domain-of-attraction: The theorem places the normal law in the domain of attraction of the Gumbel law.

A [distribution function](c:distribution-function) $F$ lies in the maximum domain of attraction of $G$, written $F\in\mathrm{MDA}(G)$, when for [iid random variables](c:iid-random-variables) $X_1,X_2,\dots$ with distribution function $F$ and $M_n=\max(X_1,\dots,X_n)$ there are constants $a_n>0$ and $b_n\in\mathbb{R}$ with $(M_n-b_n)/a_n\to G$ in distribution. Equivalently, $F(a_nx+b_n)^n\to G(x)$ for every real $x$.

statement: Let $(\xi_n)$ be a [stationary sequence](c:stationary-sequence) with maxima $M_n$. If $a_n(M_n - b_n)$ has a non-degenerate limit law $G$ in [distribution](c:convergence-in-distribution) and Leadbetter's condition $D(u_n)$ holds at the levels $u_n = x/a_n + b_n$, then $G$ is an [extreme value distribution](c:extreme-value-distribution).

hypotheses.text: The sequence $(\xi_n)$ is a [stationary sequence](c:stationary-sequence).
There are constants $a_n > 0$ and $b_n$ such that $P(a_n(M_n - b_n) \le x) \to G(x)$ at the continuity points of a non-degenerate [distribution function](c:distribution-function) $G$.

For every real $x$ the condition $D(u_n)$ holds at $u_n = x/a_n + b_n$: the events $\{\xi_i \le u_n, i \in I\}$ and $\{\xi_j \le u_n, j \in J\}$ are nearly independent when $I$ and $J$ are separated by a gap $l_n = o(n)$.

conclusion: For every $k$ there are $\alpha_k > 0$ and $\beta_k$ with $G^k(\alpha_k x + \beta_k) = G(x)$, so $G$ has the type of a [Gumbel](c:gumbel-distribution), [Fréchet](c:frechet-distribution) or Weibull law.

proofs.name: Block approximation and max-stability
proofs.slogan: Split the sample into $k$ nearly independent blocks to show that the limit law is max-stable, then classify the max-stable laws.
proofs.scope: Outline of the published proof. The hypothesis asks for $D(u_n)$ at every real $x$, which is slightly stronger than the source.

roles.why: Stationarity makes all $k$ blocks of length $n$ have the same maximum law as $M_n$.
The limit $G$ along the subsequence $nk$ gives the second limit $G^{1/k}$.
Condition $D(u_n)$ makes the block maxima nearly independent.

steps.slogan: Approximate the maximum of $nk$ terms by $k$ independent block maxima.
steps.detail: Lemma 2.1.1 of the source, with a fixed number $k$ of blocks, gives $P(M_{nk} \le u_{nk}) - P^k(M_n \le u_{nk}) \to 0$ for $u_m = x/a_m + b_m$, because $D(u_m)$ holds at these levels.

steps.slogan: Find the limit law of $M_n$ under the normalization of $M_{nk}$.
steps.detail: The left term tends to $G(x)$ along the subsequence $nk$. So $P(a_{nk}(M_n - b_{nk}) \le x) \to G(x)^{1/k}$ at every continuity point of $G$.

steps.slogan: Compare the two normalizations of $M_n$ by convergence of types.
steps.detail: Both normalizations of $M_n$ converge to non-degenerate laws. The convergence of types theorem gives $G^{1/k}(x) = G(\alpha_k x + \beta_k)$, that is $G^k(\alpha_k x + \beta_k) = G(x)$ for every $k$.

steps.slogan: Classify the max-stable laws as the three extreme value types.
steps.detail: The analytic half of the i.i.d. [extreme value](c:extreme-value-distribution) theorem shows that a non-degenerate max-stable law has the type of a [Gumbel](c:gumbel-distribution), [Fréchet](c:frechet-distribution) or Weibull law.

concepts.c:stationary-sequence: Stationarity gives every block the same maximum law as the first block.
concepts.c:convergence-in-distribution: The hypothesis and the two normalizations of the maximum are statements about convergence in distribution.
concepts.c:extreme-value-distribution: The extreme value distributions are the only possible non-degenerate limits.
concepts.c:distribution-function: The limit G is a non-degenerate distribution function, and max-stability is an identity between distribution functions.
concepts.c:gumbel-distribution: The Gumbel law is the extreme value type for light tails such as the normal tail.
concepts.c:frechet-distribution: The Fréchet law is the extreme value type for regularly varying heavy tails.

new_concepts.name: extreme value distribution
new_concepts.reminder: An extreme value distribution is a nondegenerate limit law of affinely normalized maxima of iid random variables.
new_concepts.definition: A nondegenerate [distribution function](c:distribution-function) $G$ is an extreme value distribution when there are [iid random variables](c:iid-random-variables) $X_1,X_2,\dots$ and constants $a_n>0$ and $b_n$ such that $(\max_{i\le n}X_i-b_n)/a_n$ [converges in distribution](c:convergence-in-distribution) to $G$. By the Fisher–Tippett–Gnedenko theorem, these are exactly the laws $G_\xi(ax+b)$ with $a>0$, $b\in\mathbb{R}$, $G_\xi(x)=\exp(-(1+\xi x)^{-1/\xi})$ where $1+\xi x>0$, and $G_0(x)=\exp(-e^{-x})$. The shapes $\xi=0$, $\xi>0$ and $\xi<0$ give the Gumbel, Fréchet and reversed Weibull types.

new_concepts.name: Frechet distribution
new_concepts.reminder: The Fréchet distribution with index $\alpha$ has distribution function $\exp(-x^{-\alpha})$ for $x>0$ and governs maxima of heavy tails.
new_concepts.definition: For $\alpha>0$, the Fréchet distribution $\Phi_\alpha$ is the law on $(0,\infty)$ with [distribution function](c:distribution-function) $\Phi_\alpha(x)=\exp(-x^{-\alpha})$ for $x>0$ and $\Phi_\alpha(x)=0$ for $x\le0$. It is the [extreme value distribution](c:extreme-value-distribution) with shape $\xi=1/\alpha$, up to an affine change of variable. Its moment $E[X^p]=\Gamma(1-p/\alpha)$ is finite exactly when $p<\alpha$.

new_concepts.name: Gumbel distribution
new_concepts.reminder: The Gumbel distribution has distribution function $\exp(-e^{-x})$ on $\mathbb{R}$ and is the limit law of many normalized maxima.
new_concepts.definition: The standard Gumbel distribution is the probability law on $\mathbb{R}$ with [distribution function](c:distribution-function) $\Lambda(x)=\exp(-e^{-x})$. Its density is $e^{-x}\exp(-e^{-x})$, its mean is the Euler–Mascheroni constant $\gamma\approx0.5772$, and its variance is $\pi^2/6$. It is the [extreme value distribution](c:extreme-value-distribution) with shape $\xi=0$.

new_concepts.name: stationary sequence
new_concepts.reminder: A stationary sequence has joint laws that do not change when you shift time.
new_concepts.definition: A sequence $(X_n)_{n\ge0}$ of [random variables](c:random-variable) is (strictly) stationary when the shifted sequence $(X_{n+k})_{n\ge0}$ has the same law as $(X_n)_{n\ge0}$ for every $k\ge0$. Equivalently, every [finite-dimensional distribution](c:finite-dimensional-distribution) is invariant under time shift: $(X_{n_1+k},\dots,X_{n_m+k})$ has the law of $(X_{n_1},\dots,X_{n_m})$ for all indices $n_1,\dots,n_m$ and all $k\ge0$.

statement: If a [stationary sequence](c:stationary-sequence) has [extremal index](c:extremal-index) $\theta > 0$, then its normalized maxima $a_n(M_n - b_n)$ converge in [distribution](c:convergence-in-distribution) to $G^\theta$ exactly when the maxima of the associated [iid sequence](c:iid-random-variables) converge to $G$.

hypotheses.text: The sequence $(\xi_n)$ is a [stationary sequence](c:stationary-sequence) with marginal [distribution function](c:distribution-function) $F$, and $(\hat\xi_n)$ is [iid](c:iid-random-variables) with the same $F$.
The sequence has [extremal index](c:extremal-index) $\theta$: for each $\tau > 0$ there are levels $u_n(\tau)$ with $n(1 - F(u_n(\tau))) \to \tau$ and $P(M_n \le u_n(\tau)) \to e^{-\theta\tau}$.
The extremal index is positive: $\theta > 0$.

conclusion: $0 \le \theta \le 1$, and $P(a_n(\hat M_n - b_n) \le x) \to G(x)$ at the continuity points of $G$ if and only if $P(a_n(M_n - b_n) \le x) \to G(x)^\theta$ there. If $G$ is an [extreme value distribution](c:extreme-value-distribution), then $G^\theta$ has the same type.

proofs.name: Level equivalence through the exceedance count
proofs.slogan: Both limits are functions of the mean exceedance count $n(1-F(v_n))$, which the iid limit fixes and the dependent limit recovers when $\theta > 0$.
proofs.scope: The full statement, written out from the arguments that the source gives or attributes to Leadbetter (1983).

roles.why: Stationarity gives every $\xi_i$ the law $F$, so the union bound over $n$ terms involves $n(1 - F)$.
The reference levels $u_n(\tau)$ give the limit $e^{-\theta\tau}$ to compare with.
A positive $\theta$ forces the limit $0$ when the exceedance count is infinite and makes $\tau \mapsto e^{-\theta\tau}$ injective.

steps.slogan: Bound the extremal index by one with the union bound.
steps.detail: The union bound gives $P(M_n \le u_n(\tau)) \ge 1 - n(1 - F(u_n(\tau))) \to 1 - \tau$, so $e^{-\theta\tau} \ge 1 - \tau$ for all $\tau > 0$, and $\tau \downarrow 0$ gives $\theta \le 1$.

steps.slogan: Show that the dependent limit at level $v_n$ depends only on $n(1-F(v_n))$.
steps.detail: The union bound gives $|P(M_n \le v_n) - P(M_n \le u_n(\tau))| \le |n(1-F(v_n)) - n(1-F(u_n(\tau)))|$, so $n(1 - F(v_n)) \to \tau$ gives the limit $e^{-\theta\tau}$.

steps.slogan: Translate the iid limit of $F(v_n)^n$ into the limit of $n(1-F(v_n))$.
steps.detail: For the iid maxima, $F(v_n)^n \to e^{-\tau}$ if and only if $n(1 - F(v_n)) \to \tau$, for $0 \le \tau \le \infty$, also along subsequences.

steps.slogan: Derive the dependent limit $\rho^\theta$ from the iid limit $\rho$ in three cases.
steps.detail: With $\tau = -\log\rho$, the case $0 < \tau < \infty$ follows from the level step. The case $\tau = 0$ follows from the union bound, and the case $\tau = \infty$ from comparison with $u_n(\sigma)$ for large $\sigma$.

steps.slogan: Recover the iid limit from the dependent limit along subsequences.
steps.detail: Along a subsequence with $n(1-F(v_n)) \to \tau'$, the forward step gives $e^{-\theta\tau'} = \rho^\theta$, so $e^{-\tau'} = \rho$ for every such subsequence.

steps.slogan: Apply the level equivalence at the levels $x/a_n + b_n$ to get $G^\theta$.
steps.detail: With $v_n = x/a_n + b_n$ and $\rho = G(x)$ the two directions give the theorem, because $G$ and $G^\theta$ have the same continuity points when $\theta > 0$.

concepts.c:stationary-sequence: Stationarity gives every term the same law, which the union bound needs.
concepts.c:extremal-index: The extremal index is the power that links the dependent and the independent limits.
concepts.c:convergence-in-distribution: The conclusion compares two statements of convergence in distribution for normalized maxima.
concepts.c:iid-random-variables: The associated iid sequence gives the reference limit G.
concepts.c:distribution-function: The marginal distribution function F defines the exceedance count n(1 − F(v_n)).
concepts.c:extreme-value-distribution: A power of an extreme value law has the same type, so the type of the limit does not change.

new_concepts.name: extremal index
new_concepts.reminder: The extremal index $\theta\in[0,1]$ of a stationary sequence measures how much its large values cluster.
new_concepts.definition: Let $(X_n)$ be a [stationary sequence](c:stationary-sequence) with marginal [distribution function](c:distribution-function) $F$ and $M_n=\max(X_1,\dots,X_n)$. A number $\theta\in[0,1]$ is the extremal index of $(X_n)$ when for every $\tau>0$ there are levels $u_n(\tau)$ with $n(1-F(u_n(\tau)))\to\tau$ and $P(M_n\le u_n(\tau))\to e^{-\theta\tau}$. Under mixing conditions and for $\theta>0$, $1/\theta$ is the limiting mean size of a cluster of exceedances of a high level.
