statement: If $X \overset{d}{=} AX + B$ with $A \ge 0$, $E A^\kappa = 1$, $E A^\kappa \log^+ A < \infty$, $E|B|^\kappa < \infty$ and $\log A$ nonarithmetic, then $X$ has a [heavy](c:heavy-tailed-distribution) power-law tail: $x^\kappa P(X > x) \to c_+$ and $x^\kappa P(X < -x) \to c_-$, so the tails are [regularly varying](c:regularly-varying-function) when the constants are positive.

hypotheses.text: $A \ge 0$ almost surely, and $X$ is independent of $(A, B)$ with $X \overset{d}{=} AX + B$.
Cramér's condition: $E A^\kappa = 1$ for some $\kappa > 0$, and $E A^\kappa \log^+ A < \infty$.
The law of $\log A$ given $A > 0$ is not concentrated on any lattice $h\mathbb{Z}$.
The additive term has a finite moment of order $\kappa$: $E|B|^\kappa < \infty$.

conclusion: $x^\kappa P(X > x) \to c_+ = \mu^{-1}\int_0^\infty t^{\kappa-1}(P(X > t) - P(AX > t))\,dt$ with $\mu = E A^\kappa \log A$, and similarly for the left tail. If $B \ge 0$ and $P(B > 0) > 0$, then $c_+ = E[(AX+B)^\kappa - (AX)^\kappa]/(\kappa\mu) > 0$.

proofs.name: Goldie's implicit renewal argument
proofs.slogan: Tilt by $A^\kappa$ to turn the tail of $X$ into the solution of a renewal equation, smooth it, and apply the key renewal theorem.
proofs.scope: Existence of both tail limits and Goldie's formula, with positivity for $B \ge 0$. The general positivity criterion is not covered.

roles.why: The equation and the independence give the renewal equation for the scaled tail.
The condition $E A^\kappa = 1$ makes the tilt a probability measure, and the logarithmic moment makes its mean finite.
The key renewal theorem needs a nonarithmetic step law.
The moment of $B$ makes the error term of the renewal equation integrable.

steps.slogan: Show that $E A^s < 1$ for $0 < s < \kappa$, which gives the moments of $X$ below $\kappa$.
steps.detail: Hölder's inequality and $E A^\kappa = 1$ give $E A^s < 1$. So products of [iid](c:iid-random-variables) copies of $A$ tend to $0$, the series for $X$ converges, and $E|X|^s < \infty$ for $s < \kappa$.

steps.slogan: Tilt the law of $\log A$ by $A^\kappa$ to get a random walk with positive drift.
steps.detail: Under $P_\kappa$ the variable $\log A$ has mean $\mu = E A^\kappa \log A \in (0, \infty)$, so its partial sums form a [random walk](c:random-walk) that drifts to $+\infty$.

steps.slogan: Write the scaled tail $f(x) = e^{\kappa x}P(X > e^x)$ as a renewal equation.
steps.detail: Independence of $X$ and $A$ gives $f = \psi + f * F_\kappa$ with $\psi(x) = e^{\kappa x}(P(X > e^x) - P(AX > e^x))$.

steps.slogan: Bound the integral of the error term $\psi$ by moments of $B$ and $X$.
steps.detail: Fubini's theorem bounds $\int|\psi|$ by $\kappa^{-1}E|((AX+B)_+)^\kappa - ((AX)_+)^\kappa|$, which is finite by $E|B|^\kappa < \infty$, Hölder's inequality and $E|X|^{\kappa-1} < \infty$.

steps.slogan: Smooth the renewal equation and apply the key renewal theorem to the smoothed error term.
steps.detail: The smoothed function $\hat\psi$ is [directly Riemann integrable](c:directly-riemann-integrable-function), the remainder of the iteration vanishes, and $\hat f = \hat\psi * U$ with the [renewal function](c:renewal-function) $U$ tends to $\mu^{-1}\int\psi$.

steps.slogan: Remove the smoothing with the monotonicity of the tail $P(X > t)$.
steps.detail: The smoothed limit says $u^{-1}\int_0^u t^\kappa P(X > t)\,dt \to c_+$. Comparison on $[u, bu]$ with $b \downarrow 1$ gives $u^\kappa P(X > u) \to c_+$.

concepts.c:heavy-tailed-distribution: The solution has a power-law tail although A and B can have light tails.
concepts.c:regularly-varying-function: A positive constant makes the tail regularly varying with index minus kappa.
concepts.c:iid-random-variables: The solution is a series in products of iid copies of A.
concepts.c:random-walk: After the tilt, the sums of log A form a random walk with positive drift.
concepts.c:directly-riemann-integrable-function: Direct Riemann integrability of the smoothed error term is what the key renewal theorem needs.
concepts.c:renewal-function: The renewal measure of the tilted walk carries the solution of the renewal equation.

new_concepts.name: directly Riemann integrable function
new_concepts.reminder: A directly Riemann integrable function has Riemann sums over the whole half line that converge as the mesh shrinks.
new_concepts.definition: For $f:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R}$ and $h>0$, let $\overline m_n(h)$ and $\underline m_n(h)$ be the [supremum](c:least-upper-bound) and the infimum of $f$ on $[nh,(n+1)h)$, and let $\overline\sigma(h)=h\sum_{n\ge0}\overline m_n(h)$ and $\underline\sigma(h)=h\sum_{n\ge0}\underline m_n(h)$. The function $f$ is directly Riemann integrable when both series converge absolutely for every $h>0$ and $\overline\sigma(h)-\underline\sigma(h)\to0$ as $h\to0$. The common limit is then the [Riemann integral](c:riemann-integral) $\int_0^\infty f(x)\,dx$.

new_concepts.name: heavy-tailed distribution
new_concepts.reminder: A heavy-tailed distribution has a right tail that no exponential bound $Ce^{-\varepsilon x}$ controls.
new_concepts.definition: A [random variable](c:random-variable) $X$, or its law, is heavy-tailed (to the right) when $E[e^{\varepsilon X}]=\infty$ for every $\varepsilon>0$, so its [moment generating function](c:moment-generating-function) is infinite on $(0,\infty)$. Equivalently, $\limsup_{x\to\infty}e^{\varepsilon x}P(X>x)=\infty$ for every $\varepsilon>0$.

new_concepts.name: regularly varying function
new_concepts.reminder: A regularly varying function grows like a power $x^\rho$ times a slowly varying factor at infinity.
new_concepts.definition: A positive [measurable function](c:measurable-function) $f$ on $(0,\infty)$ is regularly varying at infinity with index $\rho\in\mathbb{R}$ when $\lim_{x\to\infty}f(\lambda x)/f(x)=\lambda^\rho$ for every $\lambda>0$. Every such $f$ has the form $f(x)=x^\rho L(x)$, where $L$ is a [slowly varying function](c:slowly-varying-function).

new_concepts.name: renewal function
new_concepts.reminder: The renewal function gives the expected number of renewals up to time $t$.
new_concepts.definition: For a [renewal process](c:renewal-process) with interarrival distribution $F$ and renewal times $S_n$, the renewal function is $U(t)=\sum_{n\ge0}F^{*n}(t)=E[\#\{n\ge0:S_n\le t\}]$ for $t\ge0$, where $F^{*n}$ is the $n$-fold [convolution](c:convolution) power and $F^{*0}$ is the point mass at $0$. It counts the renewal at time $0$, so $U(t)=1+E[N(t)]$, and some authors call $m(t)=E[N(t)]=U(t)-1$ the renewal function.

new_concepts.name: renewal process
new_concepts.reminder: A renewal process counts the events of a sequence whose gaps are independent and identically distributed positive times.
new_concepts.definition: Let $X_1,X_2,\dots$ be positive [iid random variables](c:iid-random-variables), and let $S_0=0$ and $S_n=X_1+\dots+X_n$. The renewal process is the [stochastic process](c:stochastic-process) $N(t)=\#\{n\ge1:S_n\le t\}$, $t\ge0$, which counts the renewal times $S_n$ in $[0,t]$. The $X_i$ are the interarrival times, and their common law $F$ is the interarrival distribution.

statement: Let $X$ be a continuous [stationary](c:stationary-process) [Gaussian process](c:gaussian-process) on $[0,p]$ with mean $0$ and [covariance function](c:covariance-function) $r(t) = 1 - |t|^\alpha + o(|t|^\alpha)$, $0 < \alpha \le 2$, and $r(t) < 1$ for $t > 0$. Then $P(\sup_{[0,p]} X > u)$ is [asymptotic](c:asymptotic) to $H_\alpha\, p\, u^{2/\alpha}\,\Psi(u)$ with Pickands' constant $H_\alpha \in (0,\infty)$.

hypotheses.text: $X$ is a continuous [stationary](c:stationary-process) [Gaussian process](c:gaussian-process) on $[0,p]$ with mean $0$ and variance $1$.
The [covariance function](c:covariance-function) satisfies $r(t) = 1 - |t|^\alpha + o(|t|^\alpha)$ as $t \to 0$, for some $\alpha \in (0, 2]$.
$r(t) < 1$ for $0 < t \le p$.

conclusion: $H_\alpha = \lim_{T\to\infty} T^{-1} E\exp(\sup_{[0,T]}(\sqrt2 B_{\alpha/2}(t) - t^\alpha))$ exists in $(0,\infty)$, and $P(\sup_{[0,p]} X > u) = H_\alpha p u^{2/\alpha}\Psi(u)(1+o(1))$, where $\Psi$ is the tail of the standard [normal distribution](c:normal-distribution).

proofs.name: Pickands' double sum method
proofs.slogan: Cut the interval into pieces of length $T u^{-2/\alpha}$, use the local asymptotics on each piece, and show that pairs of pieces add a negligible double sum.
proofs.scope: The full statement, with the local asymptotics and the bound for pairs of intervals taken from the source.

roles.why: Stationarity makes all pieces equivalent, and Gaussianity gives the local limit and the Borell inequality.
The local power law fixes the scale $u^{-2/\alpha}$ and the limit process with drift $-t^\alpha$.
The condition $r < 1$ away from $0$ makes far pairs of pieces almost never exceed together.

steps.slogan: Find the exceedance probability of one short piece of length $T u^{-2/\alpha}$.
steps.detail: Lemma 4 of the source gives $P(\sup_{[0, u^{-2/\alpha}T]} X > u) \sim H(T)\Psi(u)$ with $H(T) = E\exp\sup_{[0,T]}\chi$, by conditioning on the value at the left end.

steps.slogan: Bound the probability above by the sum over all pieces.
steps.detail: The union bound and stationarity give the upper bound $(H(T)/T)\, p\, u^{2/\alpha}\Psi(u)(1+o(1))$ for every $T$.

steps.slogan: Show that pairs of distant pieces add a negligible double sum.
steps.detail: For pieces at distance at least $\epsilon/4$ the variance of $X(t) + X(s)$ is at most $4 - \delta$, and the Borell inequality makes these joint exceedances smaller than $\Psi(u)$ by a factor $e^{-cu^2}$.

steps.slogan: Bound pairs of close and adjacent pieces with the pair lemma of the source.
steps.detail: Lemma 5 of the source bounds a pair at gap $(k-1)T u^{-2/\alpha}$ by a constant times $e^{-(k-1)^\alpha T^\alpha/8}\Psi(u)$. Adjacent pieces are split, so their contribution per piece is $O(\sqrt T)$ times $\Psi(u)$.

steps.slogan: Prove that the Pickands constant is positive with every second piece.
steps.detail: On the union of the even pieces there are no adjacent pairs, so the Bonferroni bound gives a lower bound of order $H(S)/(2S) > 0$ per unit length.

steps.slogan: Squeeze the ratio between the upper and lower bounds as $T \to \infty$.
steps.detail: The lower bound $H(T)/T - e(T)$ with $e(T) \to 0$ and the upper bound $H(T)/T$ force $H(T)/T$ to converge to a finite limit $H_\alpha$, which is the limit of the ratio and is positive.

concepts.c:stationary-process: Stationarity makes the exceedance probabilities of all pieces equal.

statement: In the Sparre Andersen risk model, which extends the [Cramér–Lundberg model](c:cramer-lundberg-model), if $R > 0$ satisfies $\mathbb{E}\, e^{R(X_1 - cW_1)} \le 1$, then the [ruin probability](c:ruin-probability) satisfies $\psi(u) \le e^{-Ru}$ for every initial capital $u \ge 0$.

hypotheses.text: The claim sizes $X_n$ are [iid](c:iid-random-variables), the interarrival times $W_n > 0$ are iid, and the two sequences are [independent](c:independent-random-variables).
The premium rate $c$ is positive and the initial capital $u$ is nonnegative.
The constant $R > 0$ satisfies $\mathbb{E}\, e^{R(X_1 - cW_1)} \le 1$, so $R$ is at most the [adjustment coefficient](c:adjustment-coefficient).

conclusion: $\psi(u) = P(\inf_{t \ge 0} R_t < 0) \le e^{-Ru}$ for every $u \ge 0$.

proofs.name: Exponential supermartingale at claim times
proofs.slogan: The exponential of minus R times the reserve at claim times is a nonnegative supermartingale, and stopping it at ruin bounds the ruin probability.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for the Sparre Andersen model, together with the explicit form of the condition in the Cramér–Lundberg model.

roles.why: Independence makes each increment $G_{n+1} = cW_{n+1} - X_{n+1}$ independent of the past, and positive interarrival times make the claim times tend to infinity.
A positive premium rate makes the reserve increase between claims, so ruin can only happen at a claim time.
The moment condition makes each factor $\mathbb{E}\, e^{-RG_{n+1}}$ at most 1, which is the supermartingale property.

steps.slogan: Reduce ruin of the continuous reserve to ruin of the reserve at claim times.
steps.detail: Between two claims the reserve $u + ct - S_t$ increases, so its infimum on $[T_n, T_{n+1})$ is $U_n = u + \sum_{k \le n}(cW_k - X_k)$. The strong law shows $T_n \to \infty$, so $\psi(u) = P(\tau < \infty)$ with $\tau = \inf\{n : U_n < 0\}$.

steps.slogan: Show that $Z_n = e^{-RU_n}$ is a nonnegative [supermartingale](c:supermartingale).
steps.detail: Since $G_{n+1}$ is independent of the first $n$ increments, $\mathbb{E}[Z_{n+1} \mid \mathcal{F}_n] = Z_n\, \mathbb{E}\, e^{R(X_1 - cW_1)} \le Z_n$, and $Z_0 = e^{-Ru}$.

steps.slogan: Stop the supermartingale at the ruin [stopping time](c:stopping-time) truncated at $n$.
steps.detail: Optional stopping at the bounded time $\tau \wedge n$ gives $\mathbb{E} Z_{\tau \wedge n} \le e^{-Ru}$. On $\{\tau \le n\}$ the reserve $U_\tau$ is negative, so $Z_{\tau \wedge n} > 1$ there, and therefore $P(\tau \le n) \le e^{-Ru}$.

steps.slogan: Let the truncation level tend to infinity to bound the ruin probability.
steps.detail: The events $\{\tau \le n\}$ increase to $\{\tau < \infty\}$, so continuity from below gives $\psi(u) = P(\tau < \infty) \le e^{-Ru}$ for every $u \ge 0$.

new_concepts.name: adjustment coefficient
new_concepts.reminder: The adjustment coefficient $R$ is the exponential rate in the Lundberg bound $\psi(u)\le e^{-Ru}$ for ruin probabilities.
new_concepts.definition: In the [Cramér–Lundberg model](c:cramer-lundberg-model) with claim rate $\lambda$, claim size $X$ and premium rate $c>\lambda E[X]$, the adjustment coefficient (Lundberg exponent) is the unique solution $R>0$ of $\lambda(E[e^{RX}]-1)=cR$, when a solution exists. A solution needs a finite [moment generating function](c:moment-generating-function) of $X$ on an interval $[0,r_0)$ with $r_0>0$, so heavy-tailed claims have none. Lundberg's inequality states $\psi(u)\le e^{-Ru}$ for every initial capital $u\ge0$, where $\psi$ is the [ruin probability](c:ruin-probability).

new_concepts.name: compound Poisson process
new_concepts.reminder: A compound Poisson process adds up iid random jumps at the arrival times of a Poisson process.
new_concepts.definition: Let $(N_t)_{t\ge0}$ be a [Poisson process](c:poisson-process) with rate $\lambda>0$, and let $Y_1,Y_2,\dots$ be [iid random variables](c:iid-random-variables) that are independent of $(N_t)$. The compound Poisson process is $S_t=\sum_{i=1}^{N_t}Y_i$, with $S_t=0$ when $N_t=0$. It has independent and stationary increments, and $E[e^{i\theta S_t}]=\exp(\lambda t(\varphi_Y(\theta)-1))$, where $\varphi_Y$ is the [characteristic function](c:characteristic-function) of $Y_1$.

new_concepts.name: Cramer-Lundberg model
new_concepts.reminder: The Cramér–Lundberg model describes the capital of an insurer as initial capital plus premiums minus compound Poisson claims.
new_concepts.definition: In the Cramér–Lundberg model, claims arrive at the times of a [Poisson process](c:poisson-process) $(N_t)$ with rate $\lambda>0$, the claim sizes $X_1,X_2,\dots$ are positive [iid random variables](c:iid-random-variables) with mean $\mu$ and independent of $(N_t)$, and premiums come in at a constant rate $c>0$. The risk process with initial capital $u\ge0$ is $R_t=u+ct-S_t$, where $S_t=\sum_{i=1}^{N_t}X_i$ is a [compound Poisson process](c:compound-poisson-process). The net profit condition $c>\lambda\mu$ means that $R_t\to\infty$ almost surely.

new_concepts.name: ruin probability
new_concepts.reminder: The ruin probability $\psi(u)$ is the probability that the capital of an insurer, started at $u$, ever falls below zero.
new_concepts.definition: For a risk process $R_t=u+ct-S_t$, as in the [Cramér–Lundberg model](c:cramer-lundberg-model), the ruin time is the [stopping time](c:stopping-time) $\tau(u)=\inf\{t\ge0:R_t<0\}$, and the (infinite-horizon) ruin probability is $\psi(u)=P(\tau(u)<\infty)$ for initial capital $u\ge0$. The finite-horizon ruin probability is $\psi(u,T)=P(\tau(u)\le T)$. Equivalently, $\psi(u)=P(\sup_{t\ge0}(S_t-ct)>u)$.

new_concepts.name: supermartingale
new_concepts.reminder: A supermartingale is an adapted integrable process whose conditional mean of the next value is at most the present value.
new_concepts.definition: An adapted process $(X_n)$ of [integrable](c:integrable-function) random variables for a [filtration](c:filtration) $(\mathcal{F}_n)$ is a supermartingale when the [conditional expectation](c:conditional-expectation) satisfies $\mathbb{E}[X_{n+1}\mid\mathcal{F}_n]\le X_n$ almost surely for every $n$. In continuous time the condition is $\mathbb{E}[X_t\mid\mathcal{F}_s]\le X_s$ for $s\le t$. So a supermartingale decreases on average, and $-X$ is a [submartingale](c:submartingale).

statement: In the [Cramér–Lundberg model](c:cramer-lundberg-model) with net profit condition and [adjustment coefficient](c:adjustment-coefficient) $r$ with $M'(r) < \infty$, the [ruin probability](c:ruin-probability) satisfies $\psi(u) \sim C e^{-ru}$ as $u \to \infty$, with $C = (c - \lambda\mu)/(\lambda M'(r) - c)$.

hypotheses.text: Claims arrive at the times of a [Poisson process](c:poisson-process) with rate $\lambda$, and the claim sizes are positive and iid with distribution function $F$, mean $\mu$ and [moment generating function](c:moment-generating-function) $M$.
The premium rate satisfies $c > \lambda\mu$.
The Lundberg equation $\lambda(M(r) - 1) = cr$ has a root $r > 0$, and $M'(r) < \infty$.

conclusion: $e^{ru}\psi(u) \to C = \dfrac{c - \lambda\mu}{\lambda M'(r) - c}$ as $u \to \infty$, so $\psi(u)$ has the [asymptotic](c:asymptotic) form $C e^{-ru}$.

proofs.name: Exponential tilting and the key renewal theorem
proofs.slogan: Tilt the renewal equation for the ruin probability by $e^{ru}$ so that it becomes a proper renewal equation, and apply the key renewal theorem.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem under the listed hypotheses, with both forms of the constant.

roles.why: Poisson arrivals give the Pollaczek–Khinchine series, which yields the renewal equation for $\psi$.
The net profit condition makes $\rho < 1$, so the series converges and the constant $C$ is positive.
The Lundberg equation makes the tilted kernel a probability law, and $M'(r) < \infty$ makes its mean finite.

steps.slogan: Turn the Pollaczek–Khinchine series into a defective renewal equation for $\psi$.
steps.detail: Convolving the series with $\rho F_I$ term by term gives $\psi(u) = \frac{\lambda}{c}\int_u^\infty (1-F) + \frac{\lambda}{c}\int_0^u \psi(u-y)(1 - F(y))\,dy$, a renewal equation whose kernel has mass $\rho < 1$.

steps.slogan: Multiply by $e^{ru}$ so that the kernel becomes a probability law.
steps.detail: The tilted kernel $dG(y) = \frac{\lambda}{c} e^{ry}(1 - F(y))\,dy$ has total mass $\frac{\lambda}{c}\cdot\frac{M(r)-1}{r} = 1$ by the Lundberg equation, and its mean is $m_G = (\lambda M'(r) - c)/(cr)$.

steps.slogan: Show that the forcing term is a [directly Riemann integrable function](c:directly-riemann-integrable-function).
steps.detail: The forcing term $z(u) = \frac{\lambda}{c}e^{ru}\int_u^\infty (1-F)$ is continuous and bounded by the nonincreasing function $g(u) = \frac{\lambda}{c}\int_u^\infty e^{ry}(1 - F(y))\,dy$, whose integral is $m_G < \infty$.

steps.slogan: Apply the key renewal theorem to the tilted [renewal equation](c:renewal-function).
steps.detail: The solution is $e^{ru}\psi = U * z$ with $U = \sum_k G^{*k}$, because $G^{*n}([0,u]) \to 0$ by the strong law. The key renewal theorem for the nonlattice law $G$ gives $e^{ru}\psi(u) \to m_G^{-1}\int_0^\infty z$.

steps.slogan: Compute the integral of the forcing term and divide by the tilted mean.
steps.detail: Fubini's theorem gives $\int_0^\infty z = (\lambda/(cr))(c/\lambda - \mu) = (c - \lambda\mu)/(cr)$, and division by $m_G$ gives $C = (c - \lambda\mu)/(\lambda M'(r) - c)$.

new_concepts.name: directly Riemann integrable function
new_concepts.reminder: A directly Riemann integrable function has Riemann sums over the whole half line that converge as the mesh shrinks.
new_concepts.definition: For $f:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R}$ and $h>0$, let $\overline m_n(h)$ and $\underline m_n(h)$ be the [supremum](c:least-upper-bound) and the infimum of $f$ on $[nh,(n+1)h)$, and let $\overline\sigma(h)=h\sum_{n\ge0}\overline m_n(h)$ and $\underline\sigma(h)=h\sum_{n\ge0}\underline m_n(h)$. The function $f$ is directly Riemann integrable when both series converge absolutely for every $h>0$ and $\overline\sigma(h)-\underline\sigma(h)\to0$ as $h\to0$. The common limit is then the [Riemann integral](c:riemann-integral) $\int_0^\infty f(x)\,dx$.

new_concepts.name: renewal function
new_concepts.reminder: The renewal function gives the expected number of renewals up to time $t$.
new_concepts.definition: For a [renewal process](c:renewal-process) with interarrival distribution $F$ and renewal times $S_n$, the renewal function is $U(t)=\sum_{n\ge0}F^{*n}(t)=E[\#\{n\ge0:S_n\le t\}]$ for $t\ge0$, where $F^{*n}$ is the $n$-fold [convolution](c:convolution) power and $F^{*0}$ is the point mass at $0$. It counts the renewal at time $0$, so $U(t)=1+E[N(t)]$, and some authors call $m(t)=E[N(t)]=U(t)-1$ the renewal function.

new_concepts.name: renewal process
new_concepts.reminder: A renewal process counts the events of a sequence whose gaps are independent and identically distributed positive times.
new_concepts.definition: Let $X_1,X_2,\dots$ be positive [iid random variables](c:iid-random-variables), and let $S_0=0$ and $S_n=X_1+\dots+X_n$. The renewal process is the [stochastic process](c:stochastic-process) $N(t)=\#\{n\ge1:S_n\le t\}$, $t\ge0$, which counts the renewal times $S_n$ in $[0,t]$. The $X_i$ are the interarrival times, and their common law $F$ is the interarrival distribution.
